documents.title: AeroSense P2 — executed 96-well methods
headings: P2 kinetic fluorescence: the executed 96-well experiment
documents.original_body_text: AeroSense · executed method record · 11 October 2026 B06 · executed pilot P2 kinetic fluorescence: the executed 96-well experiment Reproduce the fluorescence time courses and descriptive well metrics reported in Results. Executed; critical metadata incomplete. Runs 904–935 were acquired on 10–11 October 2026. This is a manual-addition 96-well pilot, separate from the unrun 384-well specification that follows. Samples, experimental unit and preparation The team confirmed on 11 October 2026 that HEK293 cells were measured approximately 72 h after transfection, without G418 selection. Only this plate is currently available. The plate contains one well per condition × stimulus; longitudinal readings are technical timepoints, not replicate wells or independent cultures. The labels identify intended construct conditions and do not establish stable clonal lines. Their identity is not automatically matched to the earlier 44–48 h fixed-cell microscopy cultures. Columns 1–10 are Or7a, Or19a, Or42a, Or98a, Or22a, Or67a, Or67b, Or59b, Or85b and Or35a, respectively, each with ORCO. Column 11 is ORCO only; column 12 is untransfected HEK293. Rows A–H receive VUAA1, ethyl propionate, isopentyl acetate, 3-octanol, benzaldehyde, 2-heptanone, valeric acid and buffer alone, respectively. The confirmed assay buffer contains 140 mM NaCl, 5 mM KCl, 2 mM CaCl 2 , 1 mM MgCl 2 , 5 mM HEPES-Na and 20 mM glucose, at pH 7.3 and 340 mOsm. The team reports initially aqueous VOC preparations subsequently diluted into this buffer. Final VOC concentrations are unknown. VUAA1 uses DMSO; the final DMSO fraction and an equivalent DMSO-only vehicle condition are not documented. The source report lists nominal final VUAA1 at 50 µM, without an independently verified preparation record. Acquisition and additions The report identifies a BMG CLARIOstar Plus with SMART Control/MARS and a GREINER 96 F-bottom plate. It records bottom optics, a −4.1 mm focal height, LP 504 dichroic, 20 flashes per well per cycle, 0.5 s settling, enhanced dynamic range off, temperature control off and no shaking during the response read. These are source-reported settings. The instrument CSVs directly confirm the 482–16 excitation / 530–40 emission filter labels and 12 s read spacing; they do not contain numeric gain values. At the reported initial 100 µL volume, acquire F 0a : five readings at 0, 12, 24, 36 and 48 s. Add 50 µL plain buffer and acquire the first response, labeled blank : fifteen readings from 0 to 168 s, every 12 s. The well now contains 150 µL. Acquire F 0b in the same wells: five readings with the same timing. Add 50 µL of the reported 4× working preparation, or buffer for row H, to reach 200 µL. Acquire the test response: fifteen readings from 0 to 168 s. The reported manual sequence uses an eight-channel pipette for columns 1–8 followed by 9–12. Injection timestamps and addition-to-first-read delays are unavailable. Each CSV restarts its time coordinate at its first reading; no interpolation bridges the unmeasured gaps. Header run-start times span 22:11:23 on 10 October to 00:35:25 on 11 October. The final recorded response contains a further 168 s of within-run observations. The headers do not encode a timezone. Independent calculation Each F 0 is the mean of five readings. For each 15-reading response, calculate all thirteen contiguous three-reading means and take their maximum, F peak3 . This reduces the influence of an isolated point but still selects a maximum; it is a descriptive summary rather than an unbiased effect estimator. The reported peak time is the center of the earliest maximizing window. ΔF buffer = (F peak3, buffer − F 0a ) / F 0a ΔF test = (F peak3, test − F 0b ) / F 0b ΔF corr = ΔF test − ΔF buffer The two terms use different baselines and well volumes. Their difference is dimensionless; multiplied by 100 it is a difference in percentage points, not a single test-run fluorescence increase. Time-course plots show every measured test point relative to the paired F 0b ; raw-RFU panels are also provided. No cell-free-background subtraction, gain rescaling, interpolation, fitted response or significance test is applied. Control-referenced contrasts · added 19 October 2026 Let R(s,c) = ΔFtest(s,c) − ΔFbuffer(s,c) denote the existing corrected metric for stimulus row s and cell-condition column c. Figure 14 B reports R(s,c) − R(H,c) . Figure 14 C reports [R(s,c) − R(H,c)] − [R(s,12) − R(H,12)] . H is a separate buffer-only well of the same cell condition; column 12 is the untransfected well for that stimulus, with H12 as its buffer-only comparator. These descriptive between-well contrasts use subtraction, not division by a blank. They remain dimensionless differences (×100 gives percentage points), not a new raw ΔF/F0. They do not establish a cell-free background, gain correction or matched DMSO vehicle. All 96 calculations, reference IDs and exclusion flags are preserved in the control-contrast table ; B/C retained values stay empty. Ethyl propionate B is omitted from the displayed response maps only, while C stays hatched. H and column-12 algebraic reference zeros are omitted from panels B–C. Panels A–C share a −0.6 to +0.6 scale: red denotes positive values and blue negative values, with no response classification or replicate uncertainty. Quality control, exclusions and normalization The source report identifies gain mismatch in both baseline–response pairs of row B and in the first pair of row C. Coherent shifts across wells are consistent with this concern. All 24 corrected metrics from B/C are excluded; C’s second-pair arithmetic remains available as exploratory data. The remaining 72 corrected metrics are retained conditionally. Without recorded numeric gain, this does not certify the other pairs as gain-matched. Changing detector gain changes the RFU scale, so comparisons require acquisition consistency rather than a guessed correction from untransfected wells. BMG gain guidance The independent QC table reports each untransfected stage’s first, mean and median RFU, plus the median across the twelve wells of response-mean / paired-baseline-mean ratios. These formulas are explicit. The original QC field named median_col12_F0a equals the first reading in each row; its published ratio algorithm is unspecified. The original table is retained for audit, not silently relabeled. All 96 well summaries retain unmasked arithmetic in clearly labeled *_computed columns. The *_retained columns leave excluded values empty, never zero. The source’s VUAA1 normalization is not used: it includes a negative Or7a denominator and otherwise depends on single, unvalidated reference wells. The recalculated six-well 3 SD value is an audit of the source report only; it is not a limit of detection or a response cutoff. No technical-read error bars, confidence intervals or p values are used to imply biological replication. Remaining execution metadata Reproducibility still requires numeric gains, dose and solvent preparation records, matched vehicle wells, seeding density, passage, viability, quantitative detachment, plasmid-batch identity, exact addition delays and measured temperature. The source reports partial detachment, but supplies no measurement that can assign it as the cause of a particular trace. An ionomycin-type reporter control, calcium-dependence test, localization assay and independently repeated stimulation are not part of this dataset. No doxycycline induction is inferred from the published stable-line precedent. Provenance: supplied P2 report and 32 instrument CSVs; team confirmation on 11 October 2026. This document does not retrospectively apply the separate 384-well specification. Reproduction files: guide · metadata · analysis script · well summaries .

documents.title: HEK293 microscopy analysis · 2026-10-13
documents.original_body_text:
AeroSense Results HEK293 microscopy analysis 2026-10-13 · Corrected source assignments · Pre-G418 expression screening What the images support The current dataset contains 25 technical fields across 12 image labels and 2,624 eligible DAPI objects.
The tables report fluorescence above a blank-derived threshold around resolvable objects. They do not establish whole-population transfection efficiency, viable-cell fractions, stable expression or odor sensing. Condition pools retain 9.1–22.8% of segmented DAPI foreground. This is an area fraction, not the fraction of all cells retained. Dense and overlapping regions are excluded; accepted objects are not guaranteed to equal individual cells. Fields share one experimental record and are not independent biological repeats. Corrected labels, unchanged source bytes The 2026-10-13 source reconciliation reassigned 4 fields to corrected conditions and renumbered 2 fields within conditions. The recorded audit preserves the bytes and SHA-256 identities of all 113 source files (100 individual-channel images, 12 pre-existing merges and one workbook). This is a correction to source assignment, not new image acquisition. Results are recomputed from the corrected folders; labels below follow the current outputs. The current source manifest contains 113 files. The correction record below retains the previous-to-current mapping and its audit evidence. Original TIFF files and metadata are preserved in the prepared Zenodo release package. The image links below download pixel-identical WebP copies; original TIFF file identities remain recorded in source-manifest.json. The workbook remains linked separately. Methods Source data and experimental context The host was HEK293, as confirmed by the team. Imaging occurred approximately 44–48 h after transfection and before G418. The team fixed cells with 2% paraformaldehyde (PFA), performed no permeabilization step, and then stained with DAPI. The source workbook contains plate-layout and reagent-calculation records, including DAPI/G418 layouts and lipid-reagent mixtures. These records do not independently establish experimental execution or an assay outcome; the VUAA1/odor grids contain labels without response measurements. The workbook does not supply objective, numerical aperture, camera model, gain, acquisition software, DAPI concentration, fixation duration, or field coordinates. Neither the source TIFF tags nor the workbook establishes these missing acquisition details. The biological preparation and transfection record is linked from Experiments ; undocumented settings are not reconstructed from a literature protocol. Conservative DAPI segmentation The BLUE plane was extracted from each exported TIFF. A 3 × 3 median filter was used for segmentation only, followed by a common threshold of >128 on the 0–255 export scale and 8-connected labeling. The bottom-right annotation rectangle (x ≥85% of image width and y ≥90% of image height) was excluded equally in every field. Eligible objects had area 200–2200 pixels, bounding-box aspect ratio ≤2.5, and object area/bounding-box area ≥0.4. Objects within 49 pixels of a frame edge or whose measurement neighborhood intersected the annotation exclusion were rejected. No watershed split was imposed on merged objects. These rules define a conservative image-analysis subset, not a validated nuclear census. Segmentation has been visually inspected, but not benchmarked against independently annotated cell boundaries. Small touching nuclei or nuclear fragments can still pass these geometric filters, so an accepted object is not guaranteed to equal one cell. DAPI is a nuclear counterstain commonly used with fixed preparations. Here, fixation is confirmed and no permeabilization was performed; completeness and uniformity of nuclear labeling were not independently assessed. Fixed DAPI images do not recover the cells’ viability before fixation. [4] Reporter measurement and positivity threshold For each eligible object, the signal region contains its nuclear mask plus pixels within 12 pixels, assigned to the nearest blue connected component to limit sharing between adjacent objects. The local background is sampled 24–48 pixels from that object, excluding blue foreground; at least 100 background pixels are required. For RED and GREEN separately, the score is the signal region’s 90th percentile intensity minus the background median. Measurements use the original exported channel values, before the display adjustments. This nearest-DAPI expansion does not segment cell boundaries. Excluding blue foreground from the background ring also does not exclude every neighboring cell’s cytoplasm. Fluorescent cytoplasm within that ring can raise the estimated background and reduce an object's score, particularly in dense fields. The primary positivity threshold is the maximum of the three blank-field 99th percentiles of these object scores: RED >16.60 DN and GREEN >11.95 DN . DN denotes the 8-bit exported digital value. Alternative P95 and P99.5 blank thresholds are reported for sensitivity analysis. Thresholds are calibrated and evaluated using the same blank set, so the blank fraction is a calibration diagnostic, not an independent false-positive validation. The reported fraction is 100 × positive eligible objects / all eligible objects. Condition summaries pool these counts across fields; they do not average percentages with different denominators. “Both” indicates both channel criteria within one object's measurement region. It does not prove two-plasmid delivery, protein localization, or co-expression in a viable cell. Image processing and presentation Original TIFF and workbook files were opened read-only and verified by SHA-256 checksums. New figures use fixed linear display windows across all conditions: DAPI 0–255, GREEN 0–120 and RED 0–180; brightfield remains 0–255. The enhanced display can clip bright exported values and is used only for viewing. Original-level views remain available. No sharpening, deconvolution, content removal, generative enhancement or reconstruction of missing detail was applied. The same-field RGB merges combine the original channel positions; no registration correction was imposed. [5] [6] Web previews are resized with Lanczos resampling and saved as lossless WebP. The original scale bars remain within the full field; they were not used to infer pixel size. Object overlays mark classifications on a dimmed merge for legibility and have full-resolution PNG versions for audit. These diagnostics cannot establish transfection efficiency. Camera dynamic range and export transformation remain incompletely documented. What remains to be tested Independent repeats, validated cell or nucleus denominators, viability measurements and controlled fluorescence time courses are required for stronger conclusions. AeroSense Results HEK293 microscopy analysis 2026-10-13 · Corrected source assignments · Pre-G418 expression screening What the images support The current dataset contains 25 technical fields across 12 image labels and 2,624 eligible DAPI objects.
The tables report fluorescence above a blank-derived threshold around resolvable objects. They do not establish whole-population transfection efficiency, viable-cell fractions, stable expression or odor sensing. Condition pools retain 9.1–22.8% of segmented DAPI foreground. This is an area fraction, not the fraction of all cells retained. Dense and overlapping regions are excluded; accepted objects are not guaranteed to equal individual cells. Fields share one experimental record and are not independent biological repeats. Corrected labels, unchanged source bytes The 2026-10-13 source reconciliation reassigned 4 fields to corrected conditions and renumbered 2 fields within conditions. The recorded audit preserves the bytes and SHA-256 identities of all 113 source files (100 individual-channel images, 12 pre-existing merges and one workbook). This is a correction to source assignment, not new image acquisition. Results are recomputed from the corrected folders; labels below follow the current outputs. The current source manifest contains 113 files. The correction record below retains the previous-to-current mapping and its audit evidence. Original TIFF files and metadata are preserved in the prepared Zenodo release package. The image links below download pixel-identical WebP copies; original TIFF file identities remain recorded in source-manifest.json. The workbook remains linked separately. Methods Source data and experimental context The host was HEK293, as confirmed by the team. Imaging occurred approximately 44–48 h after transfection and before G418. The team fixed cells with 2% paraformaldehyde (PFA), performed no permeabilization step, and then stained with DAPI. The source workbook contains plate-layout and reagent-calculation records, including DAPI/G418 layouts and lipid-reagent mixtures. These records do not independently establish experimental execution or an assay outcome; the VUAA1/odor grids contain labels without response measurements. The workbook does not supply objective, numerical aperture, camera model, gain, acquisition software, DAPI concentration, fixation duration, or field coordinates. Neither the source TIFF tags nor the workbook establishes these missing acquisition details. The biological preparation and transfection record is linked from Experiments ; undocumented settings are not reconstructed from a literature protocol. Conservative DAPI segmentation The BLUE plane was extracted from each exported TIFF. A 3 × 3 median filter was used for segmentation only, followed by a common threshold of >128 on the 0–255 export scale and 8-connected labeling. The bottom-right annotation rectangle (x ≥85% of image width and y ≥90% of image height) was excluded equally in every field. Eligible objects had area 200–2200 pixels, bounding-box aspect ratio ≤2.5, and object area/bounding-box area ≥0.4. Objects within 49 pixels of a frame edge or whose measurement neighborhood intersected the annotation exclusion were rejected. No watershed split was imposed on merged objects. These rules define a conservative image-analysis subset, not a validated nuclear census. Segmentation has been visually inspected, but not benchmarked against independently annotated cell boundaries. Small touching nuclei or nuclear fragments can still pass these geometric filters, so an accepted object is not guaranteed to equal one cell. DAPI is a nuclear counterstain commonly used with fixed preparations. Here, fixation is confirmed and no permeabilization was performed; completeness and uniformity of nuclear labeling were not independently assessed. Fixed DAPI images do not recover the cells’ viability before fixation. [4] Reporter measurement and positivity threshold For each eligible object, the signal region contains its nuclear mask plus pixels within 12 pixels, assigned to the nearest blue connected component to limit sharing between adjacent objects. The local background is sampled 24–48 pixels from that object, excluding blue foreground; at least 100 background pixels are required. For RED and GREEN separately, the score is the signal region’s 90th percentile intensity minus the background median. Measurements use the original exported channel values, before the display adjustments. This nearest-DAPI expansion does not segment cell boundaries. Excluding blue foreground from the background ring also does not exclude every neighboring cell’s cytoplasm. Fluorescent cytoplasm within that ring can raise the estimated background and reduce an object's score, particularly in dense fields. The primary positivity threshold is the maximum of the three blank-field 99th percentiles of these object scores: RED >16.60 DN and GREEN >11.95 DN . DN denotes the 8-bit exported digital value. Alternative P95 and P99.5 blank thresholds are reported for sensitivity analysis. Thresholds are calibrated and evaluated using the same blank set, so the blank fraction is a calibration diagnostic, not an independent false-positive validation. The reported fraction is 100 × positive eligible objects / all eligible objects. Condition summaries pool these counts across fields; they do not average percentages with different denominators. “Both” indicates both channel criteria within one object's measurement region. It does not prove two-plasmid delivery, protein localization, or co-expression in a viable cell. Image processing and presentation Original TIFF and workbook files were opened read-only and verified by SHA-256 checksums. New figures use fixed linear display windows across all conditions: DAPI 0–255, GREEN 0–120 and RED 0–180; brightfield remains 0–255. The enhanced display can clip bright exported values and is used only for viewing. Original-level views remain available. No sharpening, deconvolution, content removal, generative enhancement or reconstruction of missing detail was applied. The same-field RGB merges combine the original channel positions; no registration correction was imposed. [5] [6] Web previews are resized with Lanczos resampling and saved as lossless WebP. The original scale bars remain within the full field; they were not used to infer pixel size. Object overlays mark classifications on a dimmed merge for legibility and have full-resolution PNG versions for audit. documents.title: AeroSense component calculations and inventory
documents.original_body_text: Archived source document. Publication links are updated; scientific text and reported values are retained. Raw and complete data remain in the unpublished Zenodo preparation package. Component calculations and inventory Return to Hardware build resources Component selection audit The audit maps all 104 reference designators to 28 functional groups. Values printed on sheet 2 are calculated below. Sheet 1 leaves C1–C11, R1–R14 and L1 values blank and does not identify U3; those entries show the applicable selection equation or manufacturer requirement instead of an invented value. Table 4. Full selection audit · 61 BOM rows Function and references Nominal value Equation and substitution Selection basis and source TIA feedback R27, C21 100 MΩ; 2.2 pF Zf=Rf/(1+j2πfRfCf); τ=100 MΩ×2.2 pF=220 µs; fp=723.43 Hz. Gain magnitude at 41/67/89/113 Hz: 99.84/99.57/99.25/98.80 MΩ. Rf sets current-to-voltage scale; Cf limits feedback impedance at high frequency. At 300 K, Rf alone contributes √(4kT/Rf)=12.87 fA/√Hz; ideal one-pole integrated output noise is 43.39 µV RMS. This is one noise term, not detection limit. Schematic sheet 2, TIA; LMP7721 Rev. E pp. 17–19, 22–24 [7] Photocurrent and input stability D5, U8 VEMD5060X01; LMP7721 Cd≈80 pF at zero bias; amplifier input≈11 pF; Cin≈91 pF+layout. Noise gain NG(s)=1+sRfCin/(1+sRfCf), approaching 1+Cin/Cf≈42.4 before layout capacitance. D5 cathode connects to IN− and anode to ground, giving positive output for photocurrent leaving the summing node. LMP7721 has 3 fA typical bias at specified test conditions. Phase margin requires its open-loop response and actual parasitics; the 723 Hz feedback pole alone does not prove stability. Schematic sheet 2; VEMD5060X01 Rev. 1.2 p. 2; LMP7721 Rev. E pp. 6–7, 18–19 [10] [7] ADC differential input network R29, R36, C24 100 Ω + 100 Ω; 1000 pF Rdiff=R29+R36=200 Ω; τ=200 Ω×1 nF=0.200 µs; fp=795.8 kHz (unloaded differential model). C24 spans AINP and AINN. Both series resistances enter the differential calculation. The network isolates sampling charge; it is not a 2 kHz anti-alias filter. U8 directly drives it; no separate voltage-gain stage is shown. Schematic sheet 2, TIA and ADC; ADS8866 Rev. C analog-input and input-driver sections [8] Digitization U9 ADS8866IDGS LSB=2.5 V/65536=38.147 µV; DC current/code=LSB/100 MΩ=0.38147 pA; ideal span=2.5 V/100 MΩ=25 nA. 16-bit, 100 kSPS device; the firmware selects 4 kSPS. Actual headroom uses U8 output limits, offsets and total DC photocurrent. Resolution is not accuracy, sensitivity or usable rail-to-rail range. Schematic sheet 2; ADS8866 Rev. C pp. 5–9, 18–20; firmware main.cpp [8] Excitation current R16, R21, R24, R30, D1, D2, D3, D4 100 Ω each; 155124BS73200 I≈(5−Vf−VDS)/100 Ω. Using Vf=3.4 V at the manufacturer’s 20 mA test point and neglecting VDS gives 16 mA; resistor power≈25.6 mW on, 6.4 mW at 25% duty. This is an operating-point estimate: Vf changes with current and temperature. Datasheet Vf maximum 3.8 V is specified at 20 mA; no minimum is given, so it does not establish a complete current range. Use actual rail, LED I–V curve and resistor tolerance for limits. Schematic sheet 2, LEDs; Würth 155124BS73200 electrical/optical table p. 2; firmware duty=25 [9] LED switching R17, R22, R25, R32, R20, R23, R26, R33, Q1, Q2, Q3, Q4 220 Ω gates; 100 kΩ pulldowns; AO3400A Vgate≈3.3×100000/(100000+220)=3.293 V; initial ideal gate current≤3.3/220=15 mA; pulldown current≈32.9 µA. With Ciss=630 pF, 220 Ω×Ciss≈0.139 µs is a small-signal estimate. 220 Ω limits edge current; 100 kΩ holds the gate low when GPIO is undriven. AO3400A specifies RDS(on)≤48 mΩ at VGS=2.5 V, ID=3 A, 25°C. Threshold voltage alone is not an on-state specification; GPIO impedance and Miller charge alter switching time. Schematic sheet 2; AO3400A Rev. 3.1 p. 2 [17] LED supply reservoir C12 47 µF ΔV≈ΣIΔt/C. Example: four 16 mA channels for 100 µs without replenishment give 0.064×100 µs/47 µF≈0.136 V. A local transient reservoir, not storage for an entire LED pulse. Actual droop depends on the boost source, ESR and wiring. Schematic sheet 2, “Place near by LEDs”; charge balance Q=CΔV TIA supply filter R31, C25, C26 100 Ω; 0.1 µF + 100 µF τ=100×100.1 µF=10.01 ms; fp≈15.90 Hz. DC drop=100 Ω×IU8; 1.1 mA gives 0.11 V. This pole belongs to the supply, not the photometry signal. 1.1 mA is LMP7721 typical quiescent current at 2.5 V; exact 3.3 V board drop includes load current and component variation. Schematic sheet 2, TIA; LMP7721 Rev. E p. 7, p. 25 [7] ADC rail decoupling C27, C29 1 µF each C27: DVDD to ground; C29: AVDD to ground. Local transient relation ΔV≈IΔt/C; no numerical droop without current and impedance. Separate digital and analog supplies feed their respective ADC pins. Placement and effective capacitance matter more than an invented signal cutoff. Schematic sheet 2; ADS8866 Rev. C power-supply recommendations [8] 2.5 V reference U7, C22, C23, R28 LTC6655BHMS8-2.5; 0.1 µF; 10 µF; 10 kΩ B-grade initial tolerance: ±0.025%×2.5 V=±625 µV; 2 ppm/°C maximum temperature coefficient. R28 pulls SHDN high. C22 input bypass; C23 output reservoir. Manufacturer requires input≥0.1 µF and output 2.7–100 µF with low ESR. C23=10 µF is within that nominal range. Reference tolerance contributes gain error; it is not ADC code width. Schematic sheet 2, 2V5_REF; LTC6655 Rev. J pp. 4–5, 12–14 [6] ADC reference charge reservoir R34, C28 0.1 Ω; 10 µF Zbranch=0.1 Ω+1/(j2πf×10 µF). The equality |XC|=R occurs at 159.2 kHz; this is not a REF-feed low-pass cutoff. The schematic connects REF directly to VREF_2V5. R34 is in the capacitor-to-ground branch and adds damping/series resistance to local charge storage. Schematic sheet 2, ADC; ADS8866 Rev. C voltage-reference section [8] [6] ADC mode and digital edges R35, R37, R38 10 kΩ; 47 Ω; 47 Ω R35 holds DIN high for 3-wire CS mode; 3.3 V/10 kΩ=330 µA if pulled low. For source termination, Rseries≈Zline−Rdriver; the schematic specifies 47 Ω but does not provide either impedance. 47 Ω provides series damping on SCLK and CONVST. The precise damping choice and edge response require line capacitance and driver impedance. Schematic sheet 2; ADS8866 Rev. C 3-wire CS-mode timing; firmware main.cpp [8] Reset and boot R15, C15, C16, SW2, SW3 10 kΩ; 0.1 µF + 10 µF; tactile switches C15 and C16 share EN-to-ground: τ=10 kΩ×10.1 µF=101 ms. V_EN(t)=3.3(1−e^(−t/τ)) for an ideal supply step. SW2 grounds EN to reset; SW3 grounds GPIO0 to select download mode during reset. The RC time constant is not a guaranteed boot delay; rail ramp and EN thresholds also matter. Schematic sheet 2; Espressif ESP32 Hardware Design Guidelines, Chip power-up and reset timing [19] Controller supply and timing C13, C14, U4 22 µF; 0.1 µF; ESP32-WROOM-32E Local bulk+high-frequency bypass. Firmware Fs=4000 Hz, N=8000: Ts=250 µs, block=2 s, Δf=0.5 Hz; 41/67/89/113 Hz complete 82/134/178/226 cycles per block. The timer updates four LED GPIOs and notifies the ADC task. D5 cathode connects to IN− and anode to ground, giving positive output for photocurrent leaving the summing node. LMP7721 has 3 fA typical bias at specified test conditions. Phase margin requires its open-loop response and actual parasitics; the 723 Hz feedback pole alone does not prove stability. Schematic sheet 2; VEMD5060X01 Rev. 1.2 p. 2; LMP7721 Rev. C24 spans AINP and AINN. Both series resistances enter the differential calculation. The network isolates sampling charge; it is not a 2 kHz anti-alias filter. documents.original_body_text: Archived source document. Publication links are updated; scientific text and reported values are retained. Raw and complete data remain in the unpublished Zenodo preparation package. Back to Model Complete supporting record Reader simulation record Optical methods and filter comparisons Gas and liquid transport methods Validation plan and simulation files Optical methods and filter comparisons Full optical model, maps and numerical checks Geometry and transport assumptions The photon-packet formulation uses absorption weights, Fresnel interfaces and Henyey–Greenstein scattering, established transport ingredients described by Wang et al. The AeroSense solver implements its own rectilinear geometry and scoring rather than running MCML. [2] The solver follows packets across rectilinear material boundaries , with Fresnel reflection and total internal reflection. It does not trace arbitrary STL triangles. The four well cavities are 4 × 2.8 mm; the floor is at Z = 43 mm and the 100 µL meniscus at Z ≈ 51.93 mm. LED centers are (±3.3, ±5.7) mm; each has a 1 × 0.3 mm Lambertian emitting area and no lens. The PD is a 3 × 2.5 mm equal-area proxy for a 7.5 mm² sensitive area, centered at (0, −0.4, 40.5) mm. The 5.2 × 4.2 × 1 mm filter is a homogeneous absorptive proxy. Refractive indices are 1.0 for air, 1.333 for liquid and 1.5 for resin; resin scattering and parasitic absorption are omitted. Actual detector geometry, filter angle response and printed-resin optics need measurement. Collected power is scored as LED power × absorbed fraction × quantum yield × (470 / 520) × collection fraction . This separates excitation absorption from the probability that a fluorescence packet reaches the finite detector. Table S1. Monte Carlo sampling budgets for the optical sweep, floor irradiance, detector collection map and additional filter study. Variation among seeds estimates numerical sampling uncertainty; it does not calibrate the physical instrument. Calculation Sampling Interpretation Main optical sweep 24 conditions × 3 seeds; 24,000 excitation + 60,000 emission packets / seed 6,048,000 packets; seed variation estimates Monte Carlo sampling uncertainty Floor irradiance 600,000 excitation packets Spatial illumination, not a measured light field Collection map 224 positions × 65,536 isotropic-source packets Finite detector acceptance, not a detector calibration Additional LED / filter study 12 conditions × 3 seeds; 3,024,000 packets Per-LED excitation rejection assumptions Main result figure : The optical parameter sweep identifies which assumed inputs dominate the conditional collection estimate. Spatial illumination and source-well mixing The floor maps in Main result figure and the transfer matrix in Main result figure resolve different questions: where the modeled light reaches the cell layer, and how fluorescence from each well contributes to an LED-tagged channel. Interpret the power and spatial results separately For the same reference assumptions, LED-on collected powers are NE 0.593, NW 0.723, SW 0.829 and SE 1.008 nW. These are not the recovered AC amplitudes: at 25% duty, the time average is 0.25 times the on-state power and the fundamental amplitude is approximately 0.450 times it. The NE floor mean upward irradiance is 4.366 µW/mm² with CV 46.2%; this is neither all-direction fluence nor a prediction of cell distribution. About 32% of collected NE fluorescence reflects after emission and remains useful signal. Artificial detector acceptance cones retain only 19.3% within 45° and 64.8% within 65°. The photodiode's quoted half-sensitivity angle is not a hard cutoff, so material and angular characterization are needed before converting this model to a detector specification. Figure S1. Detector-angle and geometry sensitivity under the idealized transport model. Do not interpret a datasheet half-sensitivity angle as an acceptance cutoff. Numerical checks · conservation, uncertainty and incomplete paths The main sweep contains 6,048,000 packets. Reported uncertainty is the three-seed mean ± one Monte Carlo SE, not a 95% confidence interval or a bound on real-device uncertainty. The 224-position collection map has a median relative SE of 17.3%. Analytic solid-angle, normal-incidence Fresnel, total-internal-reflection, scattering and material-location checks accompany the implementation. Maximum energy-ledger discrepancy is 2.9 × 10 −15 . At the 2,500-event limit, up to 0.0117% of paths remain unfinished; the worst conservative unresolved green-power bound is approximately 0.121 nW in an individual run. Extra NE runs compare 2,500 and 10,000 events; they do not establish global convergence of every geometry. Validation record — Zenodo (publication pending) · Publication checks · Complete numerical interpretation Why a fluorescence standard uses a different model The homogeneous-volume calculation represents sodium fluorescein distributed throughout the well. Its row-normalized matrix differs from the thin bottom-layer cell model because the emitting volume differs. Figure S2. Separate uniform-volume model for the planned cell-free standard experiment. Standard and later cell-comparison guide Complete methods and assumptions · Primary numerical summary — Zenodo (publication pending) · Figure-by-figure notes · Hardware decision → Full spectral assumptions, noise model and filter comparisons Separate supplied spectra from constructed assumptions The LEE curve is interpolated from the vendor's sampled transmission data [3] ; two layers use T(λ)² without an added interlayer reflection model. The source LED is an assumed Gaussian centered at 468 nm with 25 nm FWHM. The green proxy has its mode at 515 nm and half-Gaussian widths of 10 and 25 nm; it is not a measured GCaMP6f spectrum. The detector uses a digitized typical responsivity curve, not a calibration of our device. For Edmund #29-190, the manufacturer gives band specifications, not the pointwise curve used here [4] . The explicit scenario is 10⁻⁴ through 482.7 nm, rises logarithmically to 50% at 500 nm, then linearly to 90% at 517.7 nm. Average OD ≥ 4 in a specified rejection band must not be read as uniform pointwise blocking across the LED tail. Varying the assumed edge gives retained LED current of 0.0104–9.36% and green current of 71.8–90.3%; these are scenario ranges, not confidence intervals. Main result figure makes the trade-off explicit: blue leakage and useful green light are weighted by different source spectra and the same detector response. Use one geometry and noise protocol across the four cases The unfiltered Monte Carlo input comprises four LED cases × three seeds × (24,000 excitation + 60,000 emission packets), or 1,008,000 primary packets. The current unfiltered green powers are 0.7848 ± 0.0723, 0.6559 ± 0.0685, 0.8228 ± 0.0501 and 0.9558 ± 0.0772 nW for NE/NW/SW/SE, respectively (mean ± one Monte Carlo SE). Blue powers are 110.49 ± 13.81, 62.26 ± 23.85, 123.77 ± 20.89 and 124.20 ± 12.03 nW. These finite-sampling uncertainties are appreciable and are separate from the old filtered 0.593 nW reference. Each 2 s trace contains 8,000 samples at 4 kHz and 25% duty, with NE/NW/SW/SE tags of 89/113/41/67 Hz. Assumptions include electronic noise of 1.5 pA RMS per sample, 0.2 nA dark current, and ambient power of 0.15 nW plus a 0.05 nW sinusoid at 100.3 Hz, distributed uniformly across 500–650 nm. Poisson counts use 250 µs bins. Signal seed 20261011 and blank seed 20262011 are recorded; five blank records are averaged. Cases share electronic-noise draws and Poisson seeds, but different expected photoelectron counts give different shot-noise draws. The offline joint fit keeps only the four AC fundamentals. It omits DC, PWM harmonics, analog transfer, ADC clipping and timing jitter. Sixty-four noise realizations test the analytic noise calculation; they do not propagate Monte Carlo geometry, spectrum, material or biological uncertainty. The displayed corrected trace is not a reconstruction of every raw frequency component. Figure S3 shows the raw signal and corrected AC on their own scales; overlapping curves under an ideal blank are not evidence of instrument validation. Figure S3. Simulation · first 200 ms of each 2 s record. Columns are raw/ideal current, raw residual including DC and excitation leakage, and four-fundamental blank-corrected AC. The blank shares the deterministic leakage with the sample. Fixed seeds are recorded above; no uncertainty bands or measured hardware traces are plotted. Source methods and uncertainty . Ask how much the blank can change Worst raw complex leakage relative to green is 11,210.32%, 475.46%, 89.55% and 26.20% for no filter / LEE×1 / LEE×2 / OD4 scenario. Under the ideal stable blank, residual complex errors are 0.1341%, 0.0704%, 0.0849% and 0.0534%. This favorable correction depends on preserving the deterministic background; it does not remove its shot noise. In Main result figure , a 0.1% blue-gain change after blank acquisition gives worst residual biases of about 11.2105%, 0.47553%, 0.08963% and 0.02625% of the green signal. Compared with a 1% fluorescence change, those are 11.21×, 0.476×, 0.0896× and 0.0263× the change. This is a sensitivity calculation; no real-device drift was measured. Earlier monochromatic photon-budget target This separate reference calculation predates the spectral filter comparison. At 500 µW LED-on power, quantum yield 0.6 and a 10% fluorescence change, the stated photon-budget model predicts a 16.03 pW lock-in amplitude change . A chosen SNR ≥ 5 target would require repeat lock-in RMS below 3.21 pW . This is an engineering target under those assumptions, not a measured detection limit or an ADC sample-noise requirement. Figure S4. Photon-budget sensitivity. Changing quantum yield, optical power or fluorescence change changes the target; actual cells and electronics remain to be measured. English methods and reproduction guide · Numerical summary — Zenodo (publication pending) · Case-level CSV — Zenodo (publication pending) · Numerical checks — Zenodo (publication pending) Gas and liquid transport methods Surface calculation and checks The confirmed working fill is 100 µL per well. The team estimates a printed brim capacity of approximately 120 µL; the nominal CAD brim remains 140 µL. That capacity estimate does not define a new cross-section, so the calculation retains the existing CAD geometry. On the main 0.4 mm grid, equal-area gas cells centered 0.2 mm above the nominal liquid surface supply each surface mean. The saved D3Q19 lattice-Boltzmann velocity fields supply a conservative finite-volume advection–diffusion calculation. Velocity is scaled to the sampled flow; the scalar cases are not independent velocity solves at each flow. The liquid boundary has zero uptake. Sample-gas flow is independent of the PCB cooling fan. Table S2. Nominal first-gas-layer arrival times: Q = 3 mL/min, D = 10 mm²/s, 100 µL per well, 0.4 mm grid and 0.25 s time step. Symmetric pairs follow the nominal geometry. Well t10 (s) t50 (s) t90 (s) NE 6.29 18.24 49.42 NW 5.30 16.66 47.80 SW 5.30 16.66 47.80 SE 6.29 18.24 49.42 The current first-layer calculation contains 26 cases: 21 selected-shelf combinations of seven flows and three gas diffusivities (5, 10 and 20 mm²/s), two geometry controls and three numerical checks. Time zero is an inlet concentration step. t10 indicates the rise of the surface mean, not first molecular contact; external tubing delay is excluded. The shelf is retained for directional flow control and a simple integral structure, rather than the fastest modeled arrival. At 0.4 mm, the downward momentum ratios for open, original plate and shelf are 1.00, 0.57 and 0.69. This approximately 31% shelf reduction is a gas-flow proxy, not cell shear or biological safety. All 26 cases pass concentration-bound, uniform-field and global mass-balance checks; the largest relative mass residual is 9.13 × 10⁻¹². At 2.5 mL/min, the worst t90 is 60.06 s, within the tested numerical sensitivity of a 60 s target. The 3 mL/min choice provides timing margin, not a unique optimum. The surface movie interpolates saved one-second concentration maps without extrapolation. Geometry and flow comparisons each span 0–180 physical seconds. Its two chapters use the same color scale and reset the physical clock. The three-dimensional movie uses these scalar fields with saved velocity fields; marker density does not encode concentration. Surface histories, thresholds and numerical checks (CSV) — Zenodo (publication pending) · Full airflow methods and reproduction guide Full gas-flow methods, geometry sweeps and wash-in checks Velocity model: geometry is the variable A double-precision D3Q19 BGK lattice-Boltzmann solver screens 18 geometries in 28 original velocity solves: the open plenum, original 12-hole plate, vertical walls, L-shaped hoods and horizontal shelves. Air density is 1.2 kg/m³ and viscosity 1.8 × 10 −5 Pa·s. Solid walls and the stationary liquid surface use halfway bounce-back; pressure terminals use non-equilibrium extrapolation. [5] [6] The BGK collision model follows Qian et al.; the pressure boundary reconstructs equilibrium at the imposed density and copies the adjacent fluid node’s non-equilibrium part, as in Guo et al. The scalar advection–diffusion calculation below is a separate finite-volume solver. Saved fields are Stokes-normalized to 1 mL/min. Convergence requires velocity change below 2 × 10 −5 over 200 steps and mass imbalance below 0.2% for three consecutive checks. All 28 runs meet the checks; maximum reported imbalance is 0.0444%. A separate near-1 mL/min solve confirms the directional trend. The momentum proxy is evaluated 1 mm below the well rim; gas-speed P95 is sampled 0.6–1.4 mm above the liquid. These are gas-side quantities , not submerged-cell shear, biological response or tissue-injury criteria. The shelf improves one metric, with a tradeoff The original geometry screen in Figure S5 retains the rejected alternatives so the shelf choice can be inspected alongside its tradeoffs. Figure S5. Simulation · gas-lid geometry screen. This figure compares 18 deterministic geometry cases on the original 0.4 mm grid: worst downward-momentum proxy, near-liquid P95 speed normalized to the open design, and pressure loss. Cases are design alternatives, not statistical replicates; no Monte Carlo seeds or error bars apply. The separate shelf/open refinement gives momentum reductions of 30.9%, 30.1% and 36.1% at 0.4, 0.3 and 0.2 mm respectively, so grid convergence is not established. All cases use the nominal CAD gas space with a 100 µL fill. Source methods and uncertainty . Hardware: the integral shelf and the provisional flow setting → Scalar model: gas concentration is a separate calculation A conservative cell-centered finite-volume advection–diffusion solver uses backward Euler in time, upwind advection and central diffusion. The inlet steps from zero to normalized concentration 1; the outlet is convective with no diffusive flux. Walls and liquid are impermeable in this gas-only calculation. Projecting face fluxes to a divergence-free field changes the baseline velocity flux by 1.54%. Three assumed gas diffusivities, 5/10/20 mm²/s, test molecular-transport uncertainty. They are not pump settings. Near-liquid concentration is averaged separately for each well; the four-well worst t90 is used in the operating comparison. Advection–diffusion then estimates gas concentration near the liquid. The 1 mL/min, D gas = 10 mm²/s NE baseline has t90 = 149.55 s . Velocity markers are not molecular concentration, and neither observable measures bottom-cell exposure. Figure S6 : The gas-delivery curves quantify arrival in the nominal gas domain; they do not establish delivery to cells. Figure S6. At 1 mL/min and Dgas = 10 mm²/s, the NE baseline t90 is 149.55 s. Gas concentration at the liquid interface is distinct from concentration at bottom-attached cells. Choose a sampled operating point against declared criteria The operating-band study evaluates 28 combinations: 0.25/0.5/1/2/2.5/3/5 mL/min at each of four diffusivity assumptions (5/10/15/20 mm²/s). It samples gas 0.6–1.4 mm above the liquid, separately from the current first-layer calculation. The comparison requires worst-well gas t90 ≤ 60 s, port Reynolds number ≤ 3 and near-liquid P95 gas speed ≤ 0.01 mm/s. The speed cap is an engineering comparison criterion, not a measured cell-injury threshold. Figure S7. Fixed-CAD flow/diffusivity study. Gas diffusivities 5/10/15/20 mm²/s are uncertain material assumptions; the candidate is the lowest qualifying sampled flow, not a global optimum. The full time-to-arrival screen in Figure S9 shows why the operating candidate is conditional on geometry and diffusivity. The ledger includes 28 original velocity solves (18 geometries), 18 hole conditions plus 2 refinements, 9 baseline scalar conditions plus an analytic benchmark, and 28 operating points plus 6 scalar checks and 1 direct velocity confirmation. Solver counts are not experimental replicates. The supplemental ledger — Zenodo (publication pending) and operating-point record — Zenodo (publication pending) give the exact accounting. The hardware gas-path specification uses one regulated downstream pump. Vergara et al. (2012) provides the separate metal-oxide dataset context for recording delivery conditions and time/batch metadata. Vergara et al. documents.original_body_text: Archived source document. Publication links are updated; scientific text and reported values are retained. Raw and complete data remain in the unpublished Zenodo preparation package. Back to Model Complete supporting record Receptor analysis record Receptor data and prediction methods Structure preparation and trajectory checks Mutation and molecular-pathway methods Evidence record and comparison design Receptor data and prediction methods Full evidence and evaluation record What was measured, and what did we compute? The main benchmark contains 24 Drosophila receptors and 110 odorants: 2,640 receptor–odorant responses in spikes/s (neuronal action potentials recorded per second) , with no missing response or  duplicate pair ID in the curated table. A response threshold of 50 spikes/s was used for some classification comparisons; it is a project convention, not a universal activation threshold. ( [1] ) All chemical names were mapped to PubChem (public chemical database used here to identify odorant structures) ( [17] ) . Eleven original names leave stereochemistry unspecified. The full docking (computationally placing and scoring ligand poses in a receptor) ( [10] ) screen excluded multicomponent ammonium hydroxide and therefore contains 24 × 109 = 2,616 pairs; the main predictive benchmark retains all 2,640 responses. These are different analysis populations. The sequence resource includes 60 OR-family genes, including Orco (odorant-receptor co-receptor, a shared partner that forms the channel with the odor-selective OR) ( [6] ) , and 65 protein isoforms (different protein versions produced by a gene). One representative per gene and 60 monomer models from AlphaFold DB (public database of precomputed AlphaFold structure predictions) support feature extraction. A predicted monomer is not the complete functional OR/Orco complex. ( [7] ; [18] ) Generalization is tested at more than one level Five fixed split definitions were prepared. The main integrated-model comparisons emphasize random pairs, unseen chemical clusters and unseen receptors; defining a split does not mean every model was tested on it. Table S1. Five prepared holdout definitions and the generalization question each asks. A defined split is not evidence that every model was evaluated on that split. Split Question Random-pair Predict a held-out combination within known receptor and odorant sets. Odorant-cold Predict an odorant excluded from training. Chemical-cluster-cold Predict an excluded cluster of chemically similar odorants. Receptor-cold Predict a receptor excluded from training. Receptor-cluster-cold Predict an excluded sequence-related receptor group. DoOR checks data consistency The DoOR (Database of Odorant Responses; integrates published fly odor-response profiles) comparison covers 107 shared odorants and 2,568 pairs. The sequence + ESM (protein language model used here to turn sequences into numerical features) ( [9] ) model has a median within-receptor Spearman (rank correlation, from −1 to +1; it measures ordering, not prediction accuracy as a percentage) correlation of 0.938. DoOR includes Hallem measurements, and overlapping Hallem pairs were used for training. This is a consistency check with shared sources, not independent external validation or 93.8% accuracy. ( [19] ) Full candidate selection and prediction comparisons Which receptors and sequence changes are worth testing for a selected mold-related odor panel? Evidence · What happened Adding receptor sequence features improved prediction for held-out receptors. Or22a (one of the named Drosophila melanogaster odorant receptors in our design panel) ( [1] ) and Or35a showed useful target-versus-control response differences in the published data. Learning · What it means Sequence is informative, but additional structural features did not establish a reliable prediction gain beyond it. Change · What we do next Use predicted pockets (a local cavity in the receptor that can accommodate the ligand) to generate mutation hypotheses, then challenge their docking (computationally placing and scoring ligand poses in a receptor) ( [10] ) and contact explanations. Explore Design → Build → Test → Learn → Redesign Design question Curate a benchmark of 24 Drosophila receptors and 110 odorants from published measurements. Compare a project-defined panel of mold-related volatiles with control odorants; these compounds are not assumed to be unique markers of mold. ( [1] ) Build the model Combine molecular descriptors, receptor sequences and AlphaFold (AI system that predicts protein 3D structures from sequence) -derived structural features in matched prediction models. Generate Or22a (one of the named Drosophila melanogaster odorant receptors in our design panel) ( [1] ) / Or35a point-mutation models with ColabFold (protein-structure prediction workflow built around AlphaFold and fast sequence searches) and dock target and control odorants. The build consists of computational sequences and structures. ( [7] ; [8] ) Test & results For receptors excluded from training, R² (coefficient of determination; 1 is perfect, 0 matches the mean baseline, and negative values are worse) increased from 0.1125 with ligand (a molecule that can bind to a receptor; here, the tested odorant) features to 0.2325 with sequence features. The full representation reached 0.2356; its additional gain had an uncertainty interval spanning zero. An initial docking (computationally placing and scoring ligand poses in a receptor) ( [10] ) screen suggested small relative preference shifts for F34Y (residue 34: phenylalanine → tyrosine) and E196Q (residue 196: glutamate → glutamine) . Learn A useful predictor can help prioritize experiments, but a small docking-score difference does not demonstrate improved selectivity. R² describes predictive fit, not percent accuracy. Redesign Move from ranking candidates to checking whether the proposed mutations actually contact the odorant and whether their ranking survives changes in docking setup. Download plotted values (CSV) ↓ — Zenodo (publication pending) Research evidence Complete model comparisons Matched feature ablation The six feature sets use the same histogram gradient boosting (a tree-ensemble prediction model that successively corrects errors using binned features) settings, the same response pairs and fixed folds. L denotes ligand (a molecule that can bind to a receptor; here, the tested odorant) descriptors; S combines sequence descriptors and ESM2 (protein language model used here to turn sequences into numerical features) ( [9] ) ; P adds pocket (a local cavity in the receptor that can accommodate the ligand) features; D adds Vina (AutoDock Vina docking score; lower scores are more favorable in this model, not a measured response) ( [10] ; [20] ) and contact summaries; M adds multiple-pose features. PubChem (public chemical database used here to identify odorant structures) ( [17] ) identifiers, response-derived labels and split columns were excluded from the feature list; missing docking (computationally placing and scoring ligand poses in a receptor) descriptors follow the existing zero-fill convention. Sequence information supplies the clearest gain in both evaluation settings. On unseen receptors, the full model adds only ΔR² = 0.0031 over LS, with a receptor-grouped 95% bootstrap interval of −0.0316 to 0.0344. The interval does not establish an additional structural-feature gain. Table S2. Matched feature ablation using the same response pairs, fixed folds and histogram-gradient-boosting settings. R² is reported for unseen chemical clusters and unseen receptors; the small full-model gain over ligand-plus-sequence features does not establish an additional structural-feature benefit. Features Chemical-cluster-cold R² (coefficient of determination; 1 is perfect, 0 matches the mean baseline, and negative values are worse) Receptor-cold R² L 0.1307 0.1125 LS 0.3855 0.2325 LSP 0.3840 0.2221 LSD 0.3781 0.2131 LSPD 0.3837 0.2154 LSPDM 0.3779 0.2356 How the earlier models informed redesign These historical results use different representative models and feature versions. They are retained as method-development evidence and must not be combined into one model’s performance. For the matched historical HGB comparison, ΔR² ≈ 0.0175 had an interval of −0.0015 to 0.0419. Bootstrap intervals use fixed out-of-fold predictions; they omit retraining and model-selection uncertainty. Table S3. Historical model-development scores under different holdouts and representative model versions. R² and Spearman rank correlation are separate metrics; these rows must not be combined into the performance of one model. Evaluation / model R² Spearman ρ (rank correlation, from −1 to +1; it measures ordering, not prediction accuracy as a percentage) Random-pair / stacked tree 0.569 0.739 Chemical-cluster-cold / global blend 0.420 0.659 Receptor-cold / original HGB 0.229 0.463 Receptor-cold / HGB with multiple poses 0.246 0.472 Docking features did not transfer uniformly In an earlier ExtraTrees (an ensemble of decision trees with randomized splitting rules) analysis on 2,616 pairs, adding Vina/contact features raised chemical-cluster-cold R² from 0.066 to 0.220, while receptor-cold R² fell from 0.117 to 0.006. An eight-receptor pocket-redocking study and a small restrained implicit-solvent OpenMM (the software engine that integrates the atomic equations of motion) ( [14] ) study also failed to establish a stable unseen-receptor improvement. These results motivated better pocket placement, pose checks and membrane-based conformational sampling. Feature hypotheses, comparison cohorts and interpretation Purpose · connect both sides of a receptor–odorant pair A receptor sequence describes the protein, while molecular weight, spectra and learned chemical features describe the odorant. They can enter the same response predictor before docking (computationally placing and scoring ligand poses in a receptor) ( [10] ) or  MD (molecular dynamics: computing atomic motion step by step from a force field) ( [14] ) . Our baseline already combines 540 sequence descriptors, 320 ESM2 (protein language model used here to turn sequences into numerical features) features, 12 physicochemical descriptors including molecular weight, and a 2,048-bit Morgan fingerprint: 2,920 inputs in total. A Morgan fingerprint encodes local molecular connectivity; it is not a 3D structure. ( [1] ; [9] ) We asked three successive questions: does measured IR (infrared absorption: how a molecule absorbs light at different vibrational frequencies) add information; do complete harmonic modes and EVA (a fixed-length descriptor formed by smoothing equally weighted normal-mode frequencies) ( [11] ) recover information outside that IR window; and can a pretrained odor-perception model supply a useful molecular representation? These are completed prediction experiments, separate from the OR10 (odorant receptor 10 from Aedes aegypti, the yellow-fever mosquito) ( [6] ) entry/exit simulations. Method · compare the same eligible pairs within each experiment HGB (a tree-ensemble prediction model that successively corrects errors using binned features) and ExtraTrees (an ensemble of decision trees with randomized splitting rules) are two tree-based regression methods. We kept their settings fixed and used the existing five-fold chemical-group and receptor holdouts. Chemical-group holdout tests responses to excluded chemical groups; receptor holdout tests excluded receptors with known odors. Neither is a simultaneous unseen-receptor-and-odor test. Random features of matched dimensionality provide a control. Each eligible subset gets its own retrained baseline. Scores from the 82-, 85-, 67- and 109-odorant subsets are not directly interchangeable. R² (coefficient of determination; 1 is perfect, 0 matches the mean baseline, and negative values are worse) measures prediction error relative to a constant-mean reference; it is not a correlation coefficient or a percentage accuracy. Spearman ρ (rank correlation, from −1 to +1; it measures ordering, not prediction accuracy as a percentage) measures ranking, and MAE measures absolute response error in spikes/s (neuronal action potentials recorded per second) . Table S4. Eligible odorants, receptor–odorant pairs and chemical groups for each molecular-feature experiment. Each cohort receives its own retrained baseline, so scores from different rows are not directly interchangeable. Experiment Odorants Response pairs Chemical groups Measured IR / size ablation 82 1,968 53 Quantum modes 85 2,040 56 Measured–computed overlap 67 1,608 45 OpenPOM (Principal Odor Map; OpenPOM is its open-source reproduction for learned molecular odor features) ( [4] ; [5] ) 109 2,616 69 Interpretation · exploratory comparisons with grouped uncertainty Paired 95% intervals resample chemical groups or receptors using fixed out-of-fold predictions. They account for those grouped observations, but omit retraining, model-selection and assay (a defined experimental test of biological activity) uncertainty. A zero-crossing interval does not establish a reliable gain. These data and splits have been used in earlier work; this is exploratory evaluation, with no multiplicity adjustment for secondary comparisons. Measured spectra, matched comparisons and controls Purpose · test added information, not a vibration mechanism Prior work relates receptor responses to molecular volume and uses physicochemical properties to predict odor perception. Molecular weight and volume are related but distinct quantities. We therefore tested removing weight alone and removing a size-related group, alongside adding measured infrared absorption spectra. ( [21] ; [22] ) Method · 82 matched gas-phase spectra Of 110 odorants, 82 passed full chemical-identifier, gas-phase source and spectral-coverage checks in the NIST Chemistry WebBook (US National Institute of Standards and Technology; its Chemistry WebBook supplies spectral records) . Missing spectra were excluded from all compared models, not zero-filled. We subtracted the first-percentile background, clipped negative absorbance, normalized total area over 650–3,800 cm⁻¹ and integrated 63 bands of 50 cm⁻¹. The 4 cm⁻¹ source sampling interval is not an instrument-resolution claim. ( [2] ) All six variants retain the same receptor sequence features. “Sequence + IR (infrared absorption: how a molecule absorbs light at different vibrational frequencies) only” replaces the entire chemical block with IR. The size group is molecular weight, heavy-atom count and molar refractivity (a property related to polarizability and size). These removals test incremental predictive value in this model, not a causal biological effect. Published measurements Measured odorant spectra Enlarge ↗ Figure S1. Six accepted NIST (US National Institute of Standards and Technology; its Chemistry WebBook supplies spectral records) gas-phase spectra after background correction and area normalization. Peak patterns describe relative molecular absorption, not receptor activity or  absolute absorption strength. ( [2] ) Vector SVG ↓ Data CSV ↓ — Zenodo (publication pending) Results · measured IR did not improve new-chemical prediction On unseen chemical groups, adding IR changed HGB (a tree-ensemble prediction model that successively corrects errors using binned features) R² (coefficient of determination; 1 is perfect, 0 matches the mean baseline, and negative values are worse) from 0.3930 to 0.3278 (Δ −0.0653; 95% interval −0.1127 to −0.0078) and ExtraTrees (an ensemble of decision trees with randomized splitting rules) from 0.3746 to 0.3458 (Δ −0.0288; −0.0564 to −0.0003). Receptor-holdout point gains were small: +0.0028 and +0.0102, with both intervals crossing zero. Weight alone had model-dependent effects: retaining it changed chemical-holdout R² by −0.0121 in HGB but +0.0188 in ExtraTrees. Retaining the full size group improved point scores in both models (+0.0292 / +0.0751), although the HGB interval crossed zero. Weight was already available to the early response model; adding it is not an untested missing step. The table reports R². The following harmonic-mode comparison extends beyond the measured spectral window. These predictor tests do not evaluate the biological mechanism of vibrational sensing. Table S5. The method was gas-phase B3LYP/6-31G(d), a density-functional theory approximation and basis set. After checking calculation completion, mode counts, molecular connectivity and specified stereochemistry, 85 odorants were accepted: 4,767 harmonic modes, including 1,082 below 650 cm⁻¹. ( [3] ) Each molecule provides one source conformer’s complete harmonic normal modes: coordinated atom-displacement patterns near an optimized geometry, with frequencies, IR (infrared absorption: how a molecule absorbs light at different vibrational frequencies) intensities, reduced masses and force constants. This does not cover all conformers, anharmonic motion, receptor-bound vibrations or  full quantum dynamics. Twenty-two odorants lacked exact-match source files; two had imaginary frequencies; trans-caryophyllene required stereochemical review and was excluded. Method · encode the same modes in two ways EVA (a fixed-length descriptor formed by smoothing equally weighted normal-mode frequencies) gives every mode equal weight, smooths its frequency with a Gaussian of σ = 10 cm⁻¹, and samples 1–3,996 cm⁻¹ every 5 cm⁻¹ to form 800 features. Computed IR uses the same modes and grid but weights each mode by its calculated IR intensity. Neither applies area normalization or frequency scaling. This classical EVA formulation is not a reproduction of the 27-dimensional EVA used by Gabler et al. ( [11] ; [23] ) Alongside full 800-feature inputs, we tested PCA (principal component analysis, which compresses features along directions of greatest variation) compression to 16 components and random 800/16-feature controls. PCA was fitted only on distinct training odors within each fold. Its variance retention is not evidence that response information was retained. ( [24] ; [25] ; [26] ) Full OpenPOM methods, model comparisons and uncertainty Purpose · from human odor perception to insect receptor responses The Principal Odor Map learns molecular representations from human odor descriptions. OpenPOM (Principal Odor Map; OpenPOM is its open-source reproduction for learned molecular odor features) is an open-source reproduction, not the original POM model weights. We tested whether its learned chemical representation helps a sequence–odorant response predictor; a “floral” or  “mushroom” label cannot replace a measured insect-receptor response. ( [4] ; [5] ) Method · fixed 256-dimensional features, retained molecular weight We extracted the official 256-dimensional penultimate linear representation from a prespecified public checkpoint in inference mode, without response-label fine-tuning. A second fixed checkpoint was tested separately as a sensitivity comparison. The variants either add POM to the baseline (3,176 total features) or replace only the Morgan fingerprint (1,128 total); all retain physicochemical descriptors including weight and both sequence blocks. All variants use 109 odorants × 24 receptors. Ammonium hydroxide was excluded because its two isolated ions have no covalent bonds for this graph-model workflow; it was not replaced with ammonia. The upstream model does not encode stereochemistry: 109 odorants map to 106 distinct graphs, including three indistinguishable stereoisomer pairs. Identical graphs receive identical features. A provenance audit found 108 of 109 non-stereochemical structures in the public 4,983-molecule candidate pretraining pool. Exact checkpoint training/test membership is unavailable. Chemical-group holdout therefore means unseen downstream Hallem responses, not a guarantee that the entire AI system has never encountered those molecular structures or human odor labels. This Anopheles transfer study is separate from the Aedes OR10 (odorant receptor 10 from Aedes aegypti, the yellow-fever mosquito) molecular-dynamics reference system. ( [12] ) All 50 historical receptor names have candidate sequences: 46 grade A, two grade B and two grade C. Naming or duplicate-gene ambiguity affects AgOr12 (an Anopheles gambiae odorant receptor; Ag identifies the mosquito species) ( [12] ) and AgOr67. The main fragment analysis therefore uses 48 receptors with A/B evidence against 24 fly receptors, giving 1,152 receptor–receptor pairs. The initial direct-transfer baseline used all 50 mosquito receptors. Test 1 · transfer the fly-trained response model On the 2,000 mosquito receptor–odorant pairs sharing chemical identities with the fly benchmark, the ExtraTrees (an ensemble of decision trees with randomized splitting rules) transfer baseline produced R² (coefficient of determination; 1 is perfect, 0 matches the mean baseline, and negative values are worse) = −0.288 and Spearman ρ (rank correlation, from −1 to +1; it measures ordering, not prediction accuracy as a percentage) = −0.060. Negative R² means its squared prediction error exceeded the constant-mean reference on this evaluation set. This baseline does not support reliable species transfer. Test 2 · match local sequence fragments The alternative question is whether two receptors respond similarly across the shared 40-odorant panel. We compared full-length identity (fraction of aligned amino-acid positions that are identical) and ESM (protein language model used here to turn sequences into numerical features) ( [9] ) embeddings (a numerical vector representing a sequence or molecule) with local 21-, 31- and 41-amino-acid windows. Variants down-weight shared sequence framework and species signatures, subtract within-species embedding backgrounds, or require compatible relative position and hydropathy. These are sequence-based topology proxies, not a 3D pocket (a local cavity in the receptor that can accommodate the ligand) mapping. Reciprocal matching asks whether each fragment selects its partner as the best match in both directions. Activity labels were not used to learn fragment weights. However, methods were compared and selected on the same response matrix, so the selected result still requires receptor-held-out confirmation. Full-length identity gave ρ = 0.017. The 31-aa (amino-acid residues) mutual-best fraction reached ρ = 0.141 with a receptor-bootstrap (resampling observations or groups to assess statistical uncertainty) interval of 0.035–0.250. The unadjusted block-permutation p was 0.033, but BH (Benjamini–Hochberg multiple-testing correction; q is the adjusted p-value reported here) ( [13] ) correction across the tested methods gave q = 0.259. The weak exploratory signal did not meet the corrected 0.05 threshold; these correlations concern profile similarity, not individual ligand (a molecule that can bind to a receptor; here, the tested odorant) activation. Mutation and molecular-pathway methods Full mutation design, docking checks and structural interpretation Do the leading mutation hypotheses have a stable score advantage and a plausible structural explanation? Evidence · What happened F34Y (residue 34: phenylalanine → tyrosine) and E196Q (residue 196: glutamate → glutamine) lacked direct mutated-side-chain contacts in the inspected poses. Their relative preference changed with docking (computationally placing and scoring ligand poses in a receptor) ( [10] ) setup; no robust positive winner emerged. Learning · What it means A favorable score can reflect pose placement or  search choices without supporting the proposed mutation mechanism. Change · What we do next Improve pocket (a local cavity in the receptor that can accommodate the ligand) and conformation assessment before expanding mutation claims; study access in an experimentally resolved reference complex. Explore Design → Build → Test → Learn → Redesign Design question Require both an interpretable ligand (a molecule that can bind to a receptor; here, the tested odorant) –residue relationship and a preference that is stable across reasonable docking (computationally placing and scoring ligand poses in a receptor) ( [10] ) choices. Build the model Align mutant and wild-type structures, compare a common search region with an alternative template-informed center, and inspect side-chain contacts. Define preference as the docking change for controls minus the change for mold-related odorants. Test & results Using a 4.5 Å (ångström; 1 Å = 0.1 nm) contact criterion, neither F34Y (residue 34: phenylalanine → tyrosine) nor E196Q (residue 196: glutamate → glutamine) supported a direct-contact explanation in the inspected poses. Candidate preference directions were sensitive to docking setup and odor-panel composition. No mutation maintained a robust positive preference across these checks. Learn The first screen generated hypotheses, not validated engineered receptors. Lack of direct contact does not rule out indirect effects, but those effects were not demonstrated by these models. Redesign Separate the functional-prediction question from the physical-access question. Use the OR10 (odorant receptor 10 from Aedes aegypti, the yellow-fever mosquito) ( [6] ) /Orco (odorant-receptor co-receptor, a shared partner that forms the channel with the odor-selective OR) complex to test what docking alone leaves unresolved. This supports prioritizing these receptors for functional testing; their selection does not depend on a proposed mutation succeeding. The selected-panel comparison does not establish mold specificity or  a detection limit. F34Y (residue 34: phenylalanine → tyrosine) and E196Q (residue 196: glutamate → glutamine) showed small favorable shifts in the initial screen, but subsequent checks found that the direction and ranking depended on the calculation setup. Thus receptor candidates have been identified, while the proposed mutation benefits remain uncertain even before wet-lab validation.
