Raw and complete data remain in the unpublished Zenodo preparation package. Back to Model Complete supporting record Receptor analysis record Receptor data and prediction methods Structure preparation and trajectory checks Mutation and molecular-pathway methods Evidence record and comparison design Receptor data and prediction methods Full evidence and evaluation record What was measured, and what did we compute? The main benchmark contains 24 Drosophila receptors and 110 odorants: 2,640 receptor–odorant responses in spikes/s (neuronal action potentials recorded per second) , with no missing response or  duplicate pair ID in the curated table. A response threshold of 50 spikes/s was used for some classification comparisons; it is a project convention, not a universal activation threshold. ( [1] ) All chemical names were mapped to PubChem (public chemical database used here to identify odorant structures) ( [17] ) . Eleven original names leave stereochemistry unspecified. The full docking (computationally placing and scoring ligand poses in a receptor) ( [10] ) screen excluded multicomponent ammonium hydroxide and therefore contains 24 × 109 = 2,616 pairs; the main predictive benchmark retains all 2,640 responses. These are different analysis populations. The sequence resource includes 60 OR-family genes, including Orco (odorant-receptor co-receptor, a shared partner that forms the channel with the odor-selective OR) ( [6] ) , and 65 protein isoforms (different protein versions produced by a gene). One representative per gene and 60 monomer models from AlphaFold DB (public database of precomputed AlphaFold structure predictions) support feature extraction. A predicted monomer is not the complete functional OR/Orco complex. ( [7] ; [18] ) Generalization is tested at more than one level Five fixed split definitions were prepared. The main integrated-model comparisons emphasize random pairs, unseen chemical clusters and unseen receptors; defining a split does not mean every model was tested on it. Table S1. Five prepared holdout definitions and the generalization question each asks. A defined split is not evidence that every model was evaluated on that split. Split Question Random-pair Predict a held-out combination within known receptor and odorant sets. Odorant-cold Predict an odorant excluded from training. Chemical-cluster-cold Predict an excluded cluster of chemically similar odorants. Receptor-cold Predict a receptor excluded from training. Receptor-cluster-cold Predict an excluded sequence-related receptor group. DoOR checks data consistency The DoOR (Database of Odorant Responses; integrates published fly odor-response profiles) comparison covers 107 shared odorants and 2,568 pairs. The sequence + ESM (protein language model used here to turn sequences into numerical features) ( [9] ) model has a median within-receptor Spearman (rank correlation, from −1 to +1; it measures ordering, not prediction accuracy as a percentage) correlation of 0.938. DoOR includes Hallem measurements, and overlapping Hallem pairs were used for training. This is a consistency check with shared sources, not independent external validation or 93.8% accuracy. ( [19] ) Full candidate selection and prediction comparisons Which receptors and sequence changes are worth testing for a selected mold-related odor panel? Evidence · What happened Adding receptor sequence features improved prediction for held-out receptors. Or22a (one of the named Drosophila melanogaster odorant receptors in our design panel) ( [1] ) and Or35a showed useful target-versus-control response differences in the published data. Learning · What it means Sequence is informative, but additional structural features did not establish a reliable prediction gain beyond it. Change · What we do next Use predicted pockets (a local cavity in the receptor that can accommodate the ligand) to generate mutation hypotheses, then challenge their docking (computationally placing and scoring ligand poses in a receptor) ( [10] ) and contact explanations. Explore Design → Build → Test → Learn → Redesign Design question Curate a benchmark of 24 Drosophila receptors and 110 odorants from published measurements. Compare a project-defined panel of mold-related volatiles with control odorants; these compounds are not assumed to be unique markers of mold. ( [1] ) Build the model Combine molecular descriptors, receptor sequences and AlphaFold (AI system that predicts protein 3D structures from sequence) -derived structural features in matched prediction models. Generate Or22a (one of the named Drosophila melanogaster odorant receptors in our design panel) ( [1] ) / Or35a point-mutation models with ColabFold (protein-structure prediction workflow built around AlphaFold and fast sequence searches) and dock target and control odorants. The build consists of computational sequences and structures. ( [7] ; [8] ) Test & results For receptors excluded from training, R² (coefficient of determination; 1 is perfect, 0 matches the mean baseline, and negative values are worse) increased from 0.1125 with ligand (a molecule that can bind to a receptor; here, the tested odorant) features to 0.2325 with sequence features. The full representation reached 0.2356; its additional gain had an uncertainty interval spanning zero. An initial docking (computationally placing and scoring ligand poses in a receptor) ( [10] ) screen suggested small relative preference shifts for F34Y (residue 34: phenylalanine → tyrosine) and E196Q (residue 196: glutamate → glutamine) . Learn A useful predictor can help prioritize experiments, but a small docking-score difference does not demonstrate improved selectivity. R² describes predictive fit, not percent accuracy. Redesign Move from ranking candidates to checking whether the proposed mutations actually contact the odorant and whether their ranking survives changes in docking setup. Download plotted values (CSV) ↓ — Zenodo (publication pending) Research evidence Complete model comparisons Matched feature ablation The six feature sets use the same histogram gradient boosting (a tree-ensemble prediction model that successively corrects errors using binned features) settings, the same response pairs and fixed folds. L denotes ligand (a molecule that can bind to a receptor; here, the tested odorant) descriptors; S combines sequence descriptors and ESM2 (protein language model used here to turn sequences into numerical features) ( [9] ) ; P adds pocket (a local cavity in the receptor that can accommodate the ligand) features; D adds Vina (AutoDock Vina docking score; lower scores are more favorable in this model, not a measured response) ( [10] ; [20] ) and contact summaries; M adds multiple-pose features. PubChem (public chemical database used here to identify odorant structures) ( [17] ) identifiers, response-derived labels and split columns were excluded from the feature list; missing docking (computationally placing and scoring ligand poses in a receptor) descriptors follow the existing zero-fill convention. Sequence information supplies the clearest gain in both evaluation settings. On unseen receptors, the full model adds only ΔR² = 0.0031 over LS, with a receptor-grouped 95% bootstrap interval of −0.0316 to 0.0344. The interval does not establish an additional structural-feature gain. Table S2. Matched feature ablation using the same response pairs, fixed folds and histogram-gradient-boosting settings. R² is reported for unseen chemical clusters and unseen receptors; the small full-model gain over ligand-plus-sequence features does not establish an additional structural-feature benefit. Features Chemical-cluster-cold R² (coefficient of determination; 1 is perfect, 0 matches the mean baseline, and negative values are worse) Receptor-cold R² L 0.1307 0.1125 LS 0.3855 0.2325 LSP 0.3840 0.2221 LSD 0.3781 0.2131 LSPD 0.3837 0.2154 LSPDM 0.3779 0.2356 How the earlier models informed redesign These historical results use different representative models and feature versions. They are retained as method-development evidence and must not be combined into one model’s performance. For the matched historical HGB comparison, ΔR² ≈ 0.0175 had an interval of −0.0015 to 0.0419. Bootstrap intervals use fixed out-of-fold predictions; they omit retraining and model-selection uncertainty. Table S3. Historical model-development scores under different holdouts and representative model versions. R² and Spearman rank correlation are separate metrics; these rows must not be combined into the performance of one model. Evaluation / model R² Spearman ρ (rank correlation, from −1 to +1; it measures ordering, not prediction accuracy as a percentage) Random-pair / stacked tree 0.569 0.739 Chemical-cluster-cold / global blend 0.420 0.659 Receptor-cold / original HGB 0.229 0.463 Receptor-cold / HGB with multiple poses 0.246 0.472 Docking features did not transfer uniformly In an earlier ExtraTrees (an ensemble of decision trees with randomized splitting rules) analysis on 2,616 pairs, adding Vina/contact features raised chemical-cluster-cold R² from 0.066 to 0.220, while receptor-cold R² fell from 0.117 to 0.006. An eight-receptor pocket-redocking study and a small restrained implicit-solvent OpenMM (the software engine that integrates the atomic equations of motion) ( [14] ) study also failed to establish a stable unseen-receptor improvement. These results motivated better pocket placement, pose checks and membrane-based conformational sampling. Feature hypotheses, comparison cohorts and interpretation Purpose · connect both sides of a receptor–odorant pair A receptor sequence describes the protein, while molecular weight, spectra and learned chemical features describe the odorant. They can enter the same response predictor before docking (computationally placing and scoring ligand poses in a receptor) ( [10] ) or  MD (molecular dynamics: computing atomic motion step by step from a force field) ( [14] ) . Our baseline already combines 540 sequence descriptors, 320 ESM2 (protein language model used here to turn sequences into numerical features) features, 12 physicochemical descriptors including molecular weight, and a 2,048-bit Morgan fingerprint: 2,920 inputs in total. A Morgan fingerprint encodes local molecular connectivity; it is not a 3D structure. ( [1] ; [9] ) We asked three successive questions: does measured IR (infrared absorption: how a molecule absorbs light at different vibrational frequencies) add information; do complete harmonic modes and EVA (a fixed-length descriptor formed by smoothing equally weighted normal-mode frequencies) ( [11] ) recover information outside that IR window; and can a pretrained odor-perception model supply a useful molecular representation? These are completed prediction experiments, separate from the OR10 (odorant receptor 10 from Aedes aegypti, the yellow-fever mosquito) ( [6] ) entry/exit simulations. Method · compare the same eligible pairs within each experiment HGB (a tree-ensemble prediction model that successively corrects errors using binned features) and ExtraTrees (an ensemble of decision trees with randomized splitting rules) are two tree-based regression methods. We kept their settings fixed and used the existing five-fold chemical-group and receptor holdouts. Chemical-group holdout tests responses to excluded chemical groups; receptor holdout tests excluded receptors with known odors. Neither is a simultaneous unseen-receptor-and-odor test. Random features of matched dimensionality provide a control. Each eligible subset gets its own retrained baseline. Scores from the 82-, 85-, 67- and 109-odorant subsets are not directly interchangeable. R² (coefficient of determination; 1 is perfect, 0 matches the mean baseline, and negative values are worse) measures prediction error relative to a constant-mean reference; it is not a correlation coefficient or a percentage accuracy. Spearman ρ (rank correlation, from −1 to +1; it measures ordering, not prediction accuracy as a percentage) measures ranking, and MAE measures absolute response error in spikes/s (neuronal action potentials recorded per second) . Table S4. Eligible odorants, receptor–odorant pairs and chemical groups for each molecular-feature experiment. Each cohort receives its own retrained baseline, so scores from different rows are not directly interchangeable. Experiment Odorants Response pairs Chemical groups Measured IR / size ablation 82 1,968 53 Quantum modes 85 2,040 56 Measured–computed overlap 67 1,608 45 OpenPOM (Principal Odor Map; OpenPOM is its open-source reproduction for learned molecular odor features) ( [4] ; [5] ) 109 2,616 69 Interpretation · exploratory comparisons with grouped uncertainty Paired 95% intervals resample chemical groups or receptors using fixed out-of-fold predictions. They account for those grouped observations, but omit retraining, model-selection and assay (a defined experimental test of biological activity) uncertainty. A zero-crossing interval does not establish a reliable gain. These data and splits have been used in earlier work; this is exploratory evaluation, with no multiplicity adjustment for secondary comparisons. Measured spectra, matched comparisons and controls Purpose · test added information, not a vibration mechanism Prior work relates receptor responses to molecular volume and uses physicochemical properties to predict odor perception. Molecular weight and volume are related but distinct quantities. We therefore tested removing weight alone and removing a size-related group, alongside adding measured infrared absorption spectra. ( [21] ; [22] ) Method · 82 matched gas-phase spectra Of 110 odorants, 82 passed full chemical-identifier, gas-phase source and spectral-coverage checks in the NIST Chemistry WebBook (US National Institute of Standards and Technology; its Chemistry WebBook supplies spectral records) . Missing spectra were excluded from all compared models, not zero-filled. We subtracted the first-percentile background, clipped negative absorbance, normalized total area over 650–3,800 cm⁻¹ and integrated 63 bands of 50 cm⁻¹. The 4 cm⁻¹ source sampling interval is not an instrument-resolution claim. ( [2] ) All six variants retain the same receptor sequence features. “Sequence + IR (infrared absorption: how a molecule absorbs light at different vibrational frequencies) only” replaces the entire chemical block with IR. The size group is molecular weight, heavy-atom count and molar refractivity (a property related to polarizability and size). These removals test incremental predictive value in this model, not a causal biological effect. Published measurements Measured odorant spectra Enlarge ↗ Figure S1. Six accepted NIST (US National Institute of Standards and Technology; its Chemistry WebBook supplies spectral records) gas-phase spectra after background correction and area normalization. Peak patterns describe relative molecular absorption, not receptor activity or  absolute absorption strength. Receptor-holdout point gains were small: +0.0028 and +0.0102, with both intervals crossing zero. Weight alone had model-dependent effects: retaining it changed chemical-holdout R² by −0.0121 in HGB but +0.0188 in ExtraTrees. Retaining the full size group improved point scores in both models (+0.0292 / +0.0751), although the HGB interval crossed zero. Weight was already available to the early response model; adding it is not an untested missing step. The table reports R². The following harmonic-mode comparison extends beyond the measured spectral window. These predictor tests do not evaluate the biological mechanism of vibrational sensing. Table S5. The method was gas-phase B3LYP/6-31G(d), a density-functional theory approximation and basis set. After checking calculation completion, mode counts, molecular connectivity and specified stereochemistry, 85 odorants were accepted: 4,767 harmonic modes, including 1,082 below 650 cm⁻¹. ( [3] ) Each molecule provides one source conformer’s complete harmonic normal modes: coordinated atom-displacement patterns near an optimized geometry, with frequencies, IR (infrared absorption: how a molecule absorbs light at different vibrational frequencies) intensities, reduced masses and force constants. This does not cover all conformers, anharmonic motion, receptor-bound vibrations or  full quantum dynamics. Twenty-two odorants lacked exact-match source files; two had imaginary frequencies; trans-caryophyllene required stereochemical review and was excluded. Method · encode the same modes in two ways EVA (a fixed-length descriptor formed by smoothing equally weighted normal-mode frequencies) gives every mode equal weight, smooths its frequency with a Gaussian of σ = 10 cm⁻¹, and samples 1–3,996 cm⁻¹ every 5 cm⁻¹ to form 800 features. Computed IR uses the same modes and grid but weights each mode by its calculated IR intensity. Neither applies area normalization or frequency scaling. This classical EVA formulation is not a reproduction of the 27-dimensional EVA used by Gabler et al. ( [11] ; [23] ) Alongside full 800-feature inputs, we tested PCA (principal component analysis, which compresses features along directions of greatest variation) compression to 16 components and random 800/16-feature controls. PCA was fitted only on distinct training odors within each fold. Its variance retention is not evidence that response information was retained. The ordinate scales differ because EVA (a fixed-length descriptor formed by smoothing equally weighted normal-mode frequencies) weights modes equally and computed IR (infrared absorption: how a molecule absorbs light at different vibrational frequencies) uses intensities. Shading marks frequencies below the measured-IR window. This is not a measured spectrum or  a receptor-bound calculation. The point estimate fell, but this interval crosses zero; it supports neither a reliable gain nor a confirmed decline. ( [24] ; [25] ; [26] ) Full OpenPOM methods, model comparisons and uncertainty Purpose · from human odor perception to insect receptor responses The Principal Odor Map learns molecular representations from human odor descriptions. OpenPOM (Principal Odor Map; OpenPOM is its open-source reproduction for learned molecular odor features) is an open-source reproduction, not the original POM model weights. We tested whether its learned chemical representation helps a sequence–odorant response predictor; a “floral” or  “mushroom” label cannot replace a measured insect-receptor response. ( [4] ; [5] ) Method · fixed 256-dimensional features, retained molecular weight We extracted the official 256-dimensional penultimate linear representation from a prespecified public checkpoint in inference mode, without response-label fine-tuning. A second fixed checkpoint was tested separately as a sensitivity comparison. The variants either add POM to the baseline (3,176 total features) or replace only the Morgan fingerprint (1,128 total); all retain physicochemical descriptors including weight and both sequence blocks. All variants use 109 odorants × 24 receptors. Ammonium hydroxide was excluded because its two isolated ions have no covalent bonds for this graph-model workflow; it was not replaced with ammonia. The upstream model does not encode stereochemistry: 109 odorants map to 106 distinct graphs, including three indistinguishable stereoisomer pairs. Identical graphs receive identical features. A provenance audit found 108 of 109 non-stereochemical structures in the public 4,983-molecule candidate pretraining pool. Exact checkpoint training/test membership is unavailable. Chemical-group holdout therefore means unseen downstream Hallem responses, not a guarantee that the entire AI system has never encountered those molecular structures or human odor labels. This Anopheles transfer study is separate from the Aedes OR10 (odorant receptor 10 from Aedes aegypti, the yellow-fever mosquito) molecular-dynamics reference system. ( [12] ) All 50 historical receptor names have candidate sequences: 46 grade A, two grade B and two grade C. Naming or duplicate-gene ambiguity affects AgOr12 (an Anopheles gambiae odorant receptor; Ag identifies the mosquito species) ( [12] ) and AgOr67. The main fragment analysis therefore uses 48 receptors with A/B evidence against 24 fly receptors, giving 1,152 receptor–receptor pairs. The initial direct-transfer baseline used all 50 mosquito receptors. Test 1 · transfer the fly-trained response model On the 2,000 mosquito receptor–odorant pairs sharing chemical identities with the fly benchmark, the ExtraTrees (an ensemble of decision trees with randomized splitting rules) transfer baseline produced R² (coefficient of determination; 1 is perfect, 0 matches the mean baseline, and negative values are worse) = −0.288 and Spearman ρ (rank correlation, from −1 to +1; it measures ordering, not prediction accuracy as a percentage) = −0.060. Negative R² means its squared prediction error exceeded the constant-mean reference on this evaluation set. This baseline does not support reliable species transfer. Test 2 · match local sequence fragments The alternative question is whether two receptors respond similarly across the shared 40-odorant panel. We compared full-length identity (fraction of aligned amino-acid positions that are identical) and ESM (protein language model used here to turn sequences into numerical features) ( [9] ) embeddings (a numerical vector representing a sequence or molecule) with local 21-, 31- and 41-amino-acid windows. Variants down-weight shared sequence framework and species signatures, subtract within-species embedding backgrounds, or require compatible relative position and hydropathy. These are sequence-based topology proxies, not a 3D pocket (a local cavity in the receptor that can accommodate the ligand) mapping. Reciprocal matching asks whether each fragment selects its partner as the best match in both directions. Activity labels were not used to learn fragment weights. However, methods were compared and selected on the same response matrix, so the selected result still requires receptor-held-out confirmation. Full-length identity gave ρ = 0.017. The 31-aa (amino-acid residues) mutual-best fraction reached ρ = 0.141 with a receptor-bootstrap (resampling observations or groups to assess statistical uncertainty) interval of 0.035–0.250. The unadjusted block-permutation p was 0.033, but BH (Benjamini–Hochberg multiple-testing correction; q is the adjusted p-value reported here) ( [13] ) correction across the tested methods gave q = 0.259. The weak exploratory signal did not meet the corrected 0.05 threshold; these correlations concern profile similarity, not individual ligand (a molecule that can bind to a receptor; here, the tested odorant) activation. documents.original_body_text:
Archived source document. Publication links are updated; scientific text and reported values are retained. Raw and complete data remain in the unpublished Zenodo preparation package. AeroSense experimental protocols Record assembled11October2026 from the website’s documented methods. This is not a claim that every specified assay was executed. Status and missing metadata remain adjacent to each protocol. Shared microscopy record: WL-MIC-01. The acquisition date/operator and delivery method have not been recovered. Reporter correction, 13 October 2026: The team identifies the TH recording as “5137;TH” (TH-GFP), using membrane-targeted mCD8::GFP rather than a calcium indicator. The 11 October methods record is otherwise retained; the live methods page carries later execution-status updates. Live methods page · Measurement and calibration audit · Results and source data A01 Molecular cloning Maintain sample identity from a bacterial colony to the plasmid preparation used downstream. Three colony-plate photographs and four DNA gels document the bacterial preparation track. 01 Transform Introduce the plasmid and retain plate identity 02 Miniprep Recover plasmid DNA from a selected colony 03 DNA gel Inspect preparation quality with a documented lane map Transformation and colony selection The existing specification uses E. coli DH5α, LB and ampicillin selection (100 µg/mL), with overnight propagation at 37 °C and 180 rpm. The supplied plate photographs retain the original labels and marked colonies. Competent-cell preparation, DNA input, transformation and recovery settings, and the corresponding negative-control record are not yet documented. View the three original plate photographs . Plasmid miniprep Link each picked colony to its construct and preparation identifier. Record the purification method, culture input, elution volume, concentration and purity. The current source does not identify the miniprep kit or provide a measured yield. The earlier endotoxin-free maxiprep specification remains a separate requirement for mammalian transfection-quality DNA. DNA gel electrophoresis Undigested plasmids were loaded as paired sample lanes for ORCO, GCaMP6f and ten OR labels. All four gels used the same 1 kb ladder. Adjacent lanes sharing a construct name are grouped in the figure, retaining their original left-to-right order. The original TIFFs are retained. Each panel uses a contiguous crop and a small rigid rotation to align the wells. The original 0–255 intensity range is unchanged; no lanes are spliced and no bands are retouched. Crop coordinates and rotation angles accompany the figure downloads. These are undigested plasmids: their migration depends on conformation as well as length. The ladder product is unknown, so individual bands are not assigned kb values. Gel concentration, running buffer, voltage and loading amount are not recorded. Dates and lane maps are retained in the Notebook. [1] Construct provenance and sequence checks The earlier preparation specification names chemically synthesised, pre-cloned pcDNA3.1(+) constructs from GenScript. Its construct count must be reconciled with the Parts — wiki page publication pending record and the labels in the image dataset. Compare returned sequences with the designs, retain both insertion junctions and internal Sanger coverage, and include a read across the (GGGGS) 3 linker. The specification advises against PstI diagnostic digests because of internal coding-sequence sites. These are verification requirements, not a declaration that every supplied colony passed. Construct design — wiki page publication pending · Parts — wiki page publication pending · Notebook Read the corresponding evidence → B01 Mammalian cell culture Maintain the mammalian host under defined growth, wash, and detachment conditions. Executed, details incomplete. HEK293 cultures were imaged; passage, seeding history and a dated operator record for this batch remain unresolved. Key parameters Parameter Condition Cell line HEK293 (team-confirmed mammalian experimental host) Growth medium DMEM (high glucose) + 10 % FBS + 1 % penicillin–streptomycin Incubation 37 °C, 5 % CO 2 Passaging At ~80 % confluence Detachment TrypLE Express — 1 mL per T-25, 3 mL per T-75; 37 °C, 3–5 min Wash before detachment Ca 2+ /Mg 2+ -free PBS Method Grow cells in high-glucose DMEM with 10 % FBS and 1 % penicillin–streptomycin at 37 °C, 5 % CO 2 . Passage at about 80 % confluence. Before detachment, wash with Ca 2+ /Mg 2+ -free PBS. Lift with TrypLE Express (1 mL per T-25, 3 mL per T-75; 37 °C, 3–5 min). See Safety · See Notebook Read the corresponding evidence → B02 Transfection Deliver OR and Orco plasmids into HEK293 cells and preserve the delivery record for each image set. Executed, details incomplete. The imaged cells were transfected. The earlier electroporation specification and Lipofectamine/P3000 workbook are not enough to identify the delivery method used for WL-MIC-01. Method provenance The earlier protocol specification describes electroporation. The supplied transfection workbook — Zenodo (publication pending) also contains P3000 and Lipofectamine 3000 reagent tables, but does not establish a dated link between those mixtures and each microscopy set. The electroporation parameters retained below are therefore a prior specification, not evidence of the delivery method used for the current images. The executed method, reagent amounts and sample mapping remain to be confirmed from the experimental record. Key parameters Parameter Value Earlier protocol specification Electroporation in suspension; execution for the imaged samples is unconfirmed Cells per reaction 1–5 × 10 6 , log phase, > 90 % viability DNA per reaction ~5 µg total. OR plasmid : Orco plasmid DNA mass ratio 2:1 (not protein stoichiometry) Buffer Low-conductivity electroporation/nucleofection buffer, 100 µL Recovery Pre-warmed DMEM + 10 % FBS, no antibiotics Method The earlier specification calls for suspension electroporation using the DNA mass, plasmid DNA mass ratio, buffer volume, and recovery medium in the table.
              Pulse voltage, pulse number, instrument programme, cuvette, and named buffer are not specified in this source. Zboray et al. used FuGene HD into HEK293 stable lines [2] . That is not substituted for the AeroSense transfection specification above. Controls & critical notes Buffer-only pulse — electroporation toxicity. GFP-only plasmid — transfection efficiency. Genetic control Orco–GCaMP6f alone, without a tuning OR — should respond to VUAA1 but not to VOCs. Use endotoxin-free, low-salt, concentrated DNA. Use healthy log-phase cells and minimise time in electroporation buffer. Recover immediately in warm antibiotic-free medium. Omit penicillin–streptomycin during electroporation and for the following 24 h. See Design — wiki page publication pending · See Notebook Read the corresponding evidence → B03 Stable-line selection Select G418-resistant mammalian lines after transfection. Partially executed. A separate G418 batch was reported in progress; no selection trajectory or endpoint dataset is archived. Current experimental status. The supplied fluorescence images were acquired approximately 44–48 h after transfection, before G418 selection. A separate batch is undergoing G418 selection. Consequently, these images cannot establish enrichment or survival after selection, and the schedule below remains a protocol target rather than a confirmed result for the imaged batch. Current protocol target — not a validated kill curve Protocol target timeline. Day 0 transfection with antibiotic-free recovery. G418 at 100 micrograms per millilitre starts 24 to 48 hours later and runs for 2 weeks. Concentration is then raised to 150 for 1 week, then maintenance at about 75 ongoing. These doses are a literature-informed starting condition, not an AeroSense-confirmed kill-curve result. Day 0 Transfection Suspension transfection. Recovery in DMEM + 10 % FBS, no antibiotics for 24 h. 24–48 h G418 100 µg/mL Selection start, 2 weeks. Not added at seeding. Days 1–2: little visible effect; 3–5: bulk death; 10–14: resistant colonies. After 2 weeks G418 150 µg/mL Selection raised, 1 week. Thereafter G418 ~75 µg/mL Maintenance, ongoing. Figure 2. G418 selection timeline (protocol target). Current protocol target / literature-informed starting condition: G418 started 24–48 h after transfection at 100 µg/mL for 2 weeks, then 150 µg/mL for 1 week, then maintenance at ~75 µg/mL.
                  This is not an AeroSense-validated kill-curve result. Key parameters Stage G418 concentration Duration Selection start (24–48 h post-transfection) 100 µg/mL 2 weeks Selection raised 150 µg/mL 1 week Maintenance ~75 µg/mL ongoing Method Before transfection, run a G418 kill curve on untransfected host cells (draft range 0–800 µg/mL) for that cell lot, confluence, and G418 batch. Do not treat the table below as a confirmed effective dose. After transfection, allow 24–48 h recovery. Do not add G418 at seeding. Start selection at 100 µg/mL G418 for 2 weeks. Refresh selection medium every 2–3 days. Raise G418 to 150 µg/mL for 1 week. Maintain lines at ~75 µg/mL G418 thereafter. During the first selection window, little visible effect is expected for 1–2 days, bulk cell death at days 3–5, and discrete resistant colonies against a cleared background by days 10–14. Those timings are operational expectations, not recorded AeroSense outcomes. Controls & critical notes Negative control Untransfected well at the same G418 dose throughout selection — every cell in it should die. Add G418 24–48 h after transfection, not at seeding, so cells can recover and express NeoR. The 100 → 150 → ~75 µg/mL schedule is a current protocol target / literature-informed starting condition, not an experimentally confirmed AeroSense kill curve. See Design — wiki page publication pending · See Notebook Read the corresponding evidence → B04 Expression / functional validation Confirm cassette transcription and Orco/GCaMP function before VOC assays. Partially executed. Fixed-cell endpoint imaging was acquired; the localization and time-resolved functional tests below remain assay specifications. Current microscopy record The team confirms that the supplied HEK293 images were acquired approximately 44–48 h after transfection and before G418 selection. Cells were fixed with 2% paraformaldehyde before DAPI staining, without a permeabilization step. Blue images show DAPI. Files sharing the same field number refer to the same field of view across channels; exposure was held constant within each channel across groups, and blank calibration was performed. Fixation duration, numerical exposure settings and the complete acquisition log have not been supplied. The available fields are technical observations from one experimental batch, with no independent biological repeats and no live/dead assay. DAPI provides a nuclear denominator for an image-based estimate after segmentation quality control; it does not establish viability. Dense or overlapping nuclei require explicit uncertainty handling. Report the number of analyzable fields per sample and distinguish a nuclear-normalized reporter-positive fraction from confirmed live-cell transfection efficiency. GCaMP6f resting fluorescence and mCherry expression are interpreted separately from stimulus-dependent response and cell viability. Image analysis, sample-level estimates and limitations · Original preparation workbook — Zenodo (publication pending) Key parameters Parameter Value mCherry microscopy ex ~587 nm / em ~610 nm GCaMP6f rest fluorescence ex ~485 nm / em ~510 nm; dim at rest is expected, not a failure VUAA1 Synthetic Orco agonist used as a functional positive-control stimulus [3] Western blot Optional / implementation details pending Ionomycin Optional / implementation details pending Method Record mCherry (ex ~587 nm / em ~610 nm) versus mock / untransfected cells.
                Red fluorescence reports that the OR cassette is transcribed. It does not report OR folding or plasma-membrane trafficking. After an expression gate, compare vehicle versus VUAA1 on cells that should contain Orco–GCaMP6f.
                VUAA1 is a synthetic Orco agonist used as a functional positive-control stimulus [3] Jones et al., 2011 — full entry in References. .
                A VUAA1 response supports functionality of the Orco/GCaMP sensing chain. It does not, by itself, prove membrane trafficking. Controls & critical notes Expression control Mock / untransfected cells for mCherry autofluorescence. Functional positive control VUAA1 versus vehicle. VUAA1 is a synthetic Orco agonist used as a functional positive-control stimulus, not a proof of membrane trafficking. Optional / implementation details pending Ionomycin (reporter isolated from channel) and anti-His western blot of the RSET leader. Concentration, solvent, incubation, antibody, and whether either assay is in the AeroSense SOP are not specified. GCaMP6f is dim at rest. Absence of bright green is expected, not a failure. See Design — wiki page publication pending · See Results · See Notebook Read the corresponding evidence → B05 Endpoint microscopy and image analysis Reproduce the DAPI-object fluorescence screen reported in Results. Executed analysis. All 25 fields and all 2,624 eligible objects are retained in the published data tables and reproducibility package. Source data and experimental context The host was HEK293, as confirmed by the team. Imaging occurred approximately 44–48 h after transfection and before G418. The team fixed cells with 2% paraformaldehyde (PFA), performed no permeabilization step, and then stained with DAPI. The source workbook contains plate-layout and reagent-calculation records, including DAPI/G418 layouts and lipid-reagent mixtures. These records do not independently establish experimental execution or an assay outcome; the VUAA1/odor grids contain labels without response measurements. The workbook does not supply objective, numerical aperture, camera model, gain, acquisition software, DAPI concentration, fixation duration, or field coordinates. Neither the source TIFF tags nor the workbook establishes these missing acquisition details. The biological preparation and transfection record is linked from Experiments ; undocumented settings are not reconstructed from a literature protocol. Conservative DAPI segmentation The BLUE plane was extracted from each exported TIFF. A 3 × 3 median filter was used for segmentation only, followed by a common threshold of >128 on the 0–255 export scale and 8-connected labeling. The bottom-right annotation rectangle (x ≥85% of image width and y ≥90% of image height) was excluded equally in every field. Eligible objects had area 200–2200 pixels, bounding-box aspect ratio ≤2.5, and object area/bounding-box area ≥0.4. Objects within 49 pixels of a frame edge or whose measurement neighborhood intersected the annotation exclusion were rejected. No watershed split was imposed on merged objects. These rules define a conservative image-analysis subset, not a validated nuclear census. Segmentation has been visually inspected, but not benchmarked against independently annotated cell boundaries. Small touching nuclei or nuclear fragments can still pass these geometric filters, so an accepted object is not guaranteed to equal one cell. DAPI is a nuclear counterstain commonly used with fixed preparations. Here, fixation is confirmed and no permeabilization was performed; completeness and uniformity of nuclear labeling were not independently assessed. Fixed DAPI images do not recover the cells’ viability before fixation. [4] Reporter measurement and positivity threshold The full Measurement record adds an explicit statistical specification, all three same-batch blank-field holdouts and the area-versus-object audit. These additions leave the original segmentation and primary thresholds unchanged. For each eligible object, the signal region contains its nuclear mask plus pixels within 12 pixels, assigned to the nearest blue connected component to limit sharing between adjacent objects. The local background is sampled 24–48 pixels from that object, excluding blue foreground; at least 100 background pixels are required. For RED and GREEN separately, the score is the signal region’s 90th percentile intensity minus the background median. Measurements use the original exported channel values, before the display adjustments. This nearest-DAPI expansion does not segment cell boundaries. Excluding blue foreground from the background ring also does not exclude every neighboring cell’s cytoplasm. Fluorescent cytoplasm within that ring can raise the estimated background and reduce an object's score, particularly in dense fields. The primary positivity threshold is the maximum of the three blank-field 99th percentiles of these object scores: RED >16.60 DN and GREEN >11.95 DN . DN denotes the 8-bit exported digital value. Alternative P95 and P99.5 blank thresholds are reported for sensitivity analysis. Thresholds are calibrated and evaluated using the same blank set, so the blank fraction is a calibration diagnostic, not an independent false-positive validation. The reported fraction is 100 × positive eligible objects / all eligible objects. Condition summaries pool these counts across fields; they do not average percentages with different denominators. “Both” indicates both channel criteria within one object's measurement region. It does not prove two-plasmid delivery, protein localization, or co-expression in a viable cell. Image processing and presentation Original TIFF and workbook files were opened read-only and verified by SHA-256 checksums. New figures use fixed linear display windows across all conditions: DAPI 0–255, GREEN 0–120 and RED 0–180; brightfield remains 0–255. The enhanced display can clip bright exported values and is used only for viewing. Original-level views remain available. No sharpening, deconvolution, content removal, generative enhancement or reconstruction of missing detail was applied. The same-field RGB merges combine the original channel positions; no registration correction was imposed. [5] [6] Web previews are resized with Lanczos resampling and saved as lossless WebP. The original scale bars remain within the full field; they were not used to infer pixel size. Object overlays mark classifications on a dimmed merge for legibility and have full-resolution PNG versions for audit. Microscopy results and all-field gallery · Scripts, data and source files · Reproduce the control comparison Read the corresponding evidence → B06 Calcium imaging assay Measure VOC-evoked GCaMP6f fluorescence in a 384-well plate with a matched vehicle injection. Specification; not run. This 384-well assay has no executed plate-level dataset in the current archive. The earlier qualitative VUAA1 observation does not verify this protocol. The calcium-response assay was adapted from Zboray et al. [2] Zboray et al., 2023 — full entry in References. .
              AeroSense-specific construct, transfection, and validation procedures are documented separately above.
              Plate geometry, buffer volumes, and the two-round injection sequence below follow that published assay design. Key parameters Parameter Value Plate format Black-wall, clear-bottom 384-well Seeding 12,000–18,000 cells per well, 48–72 h before measurement Assay volume 20 µL assay buffer per well Vehicle injection 7 µL plain VOC buffer Odorant injection 9 µL of VOC at 4× final concentration Final well volume 36 µL (20 + 7 + 9) VOC concentrations 1, 10 and 100 µM final VUAA1 reference 50 µM on every plate for every cell line Instrument Multimode plate reader with a two-channel injector (model not specified) Readout ex 485 nm / em 535 nm Sampling F 0 for 5 s; then 30 s at 1 read/s after each injection Buffers Component Assay buffer VOC buffer NaCl 140 mM 140 mM KCl 5 mM 5 mM CaCl 2 2 mM 2 mM MgCl 2 1 mM 1 mM HEPES-Na 5 mM 5 mM Glucose 20 mM 31 mM DMSO — 0.1 % pH / osmolarity 7.3 / 340 mOsm 7.3 / 340 mOsm Method Read on a multimode plate reader with a two-channel injector, ex 485 nm / em 535 nm. Seed cells at 12,000–18,000 per well in black-wall, clear-bottom 384-well plates, 48–72 h before measurement. On the day of measurement, replace growth medium with 20 µL assay buffer per well. Round 1 — vehicle: record baseline F 0 for 5 s, inject 7 µL plain VOC buffer, record 30 s at 1 read/s. Round 2 — odorant: into the same wells, inject 9 µL of VOC at 4× final concentration, same recording protocol. Layout: one compound per row; up to eight cell lines per 24-column plate. Use three wells per cell line and measure each VOC–OR pair on at least three separate days. The volumes are self-consistent: 20 + 7 = 27 µL, then + 9 = 36 µL; 9/36 = 1/4, so a 4× stock dilutes exactly to 1× final. The vehicle injection simultaneously establishes the volume for the second round and measures the solvent and injection artefact alone. Well volume and two-round sequence Three well volumes. First: 20 microlitres assay buffer. Second: 20 plus 7 microlitres vehicle equals 27. Third: 27 plus 9 microlitres of 4 times VOC equals 36. Nine divided by 36 equals one quarter, so a 4 times stock becomes 1 times final. 20 µL assay buffer 20 µL + 7 µL vehicle 20 µL assay buffer = 27 µL + 9 µL 4× VOC 7 µL vehicle 20 µL assay buffer = 36 µL 9 / 36 = 1/4  →  4× stock dilutes to 1× final Round 1 F 0 5 s Inject 7 µL vehicle Record 30 s at 1 read/s Round 2 Same wells Inject 9 µL 4× VOC Record 30 s at 1 read/s Figure 3. Two-round calcium assay volumes. 20 µL assay buffer + 7 µL vehicle = 27 µL; then + 9 µL of 4× VOC = 36 µL.
                  9/36 = 1/4, so a 4× stock becomes 1× final concentration.
                  Geometry adapted from Zboray et al. [2] . Reagent preparation VUAA1 stock and VOC handling VUAA1. Dissolve in DMSO to a 50 mM stock (18.4 mg/mL). Aliquot and store at −20 °C protected from light. Prepare the 4× working dilution fresh in VOC buffer. VOCs. Dilute directly in VOC buffer, or first in DMSO for water-insoluble compounds. Prepare working solutions fresh daily. Store concentrated stocks in amber glass with PTFE-lined caps. Controls & critical notes Vehicle control Round-1 injection of plain VOC buffer — solvent and injection artefact. Normalisation reference 50 µM VUAA1 for each cell line on the same plate/day. Normalise to the mean VUAA1 response of that line, not a same-well VUAA1 injection. Specificity control Ca 2+ -free condition. Zboray et al. showed that Ca 2+ -free and Ca 2+ -free + EGTA buffers abolish the VUAA1 response [2] . Keep DMSO identical in VOC, vehicle, and VUAA1 wells. CaCl 2 in the assay buffer is required. Use HEPES-Na rather than bicarbonate: the plate sits in ambient air. Reproducibility metadata Technical replicates Three wells per cell line, one compound per row, triplicate Day replicates Each VOC–OR pair measured on at least three separate days Instrument Multimode plate reader with a two-channel injector (model not specified) Excitation / emission 485 nm / 535 nm Sampling rate 1 read/s for 30 s after each injection; F 0 recorded for 5 s before injection Analysis R then R norm ; see Data analysis See Safety · See Results · See Notebook Read the corresponding evidence → B07 Data analysis Convert raw fluorescence into a VUAA1-normalised relative response for each receptor–stimulus pair. Specification; not run. These response metrics apply to future time courses; fixed-cell image fractions use the separate microscopy pipeline. Relative-response definition, the ≤ 0.05 floor, plate/day VUAA1 mean normalisation, and Grubbs’ outlier removal follow Zboray et al. [2] Zboray et al., 2023 — full entry in References. .
              Zboray et al. denote the relative response R as Δ F . This page uses R and R norm to avoid mixing Δ F with Δ F / F 0 . Key parameters Parameter Value Raw fluorescence Plate-reader intensity at ex 485 nm / em 535 nm F 0 Baseline recorded for 5 s before the relevant injection F max Peak fluorescence in the post-injection window Raw relative response R = (F max − F 0 ) / F 0 VUAA1-normalised response R norm = R VOC / mean( R VUAA1 , corresponding cell line, same plate/day) Zero floor R norm ≤ 0.05 treated as zero, following [2] Outliers Removed by Grubbs’ test, following [2] (α not specified here) Method Record raw fluorescence at ex 485 nm / em 535 nm. Take F 0 as the 5 s baseline before the relevant injection. Take F max as the peak in the post-injection window. Compute R = (F max − F 0 ) / F 0 . Normalise each VOC response to the mean 50 µM VUAA1 response of the corresponding OR cell line measured on the same plate/day: R norm = R VOC / mean( R VUAA1 , corresponding cell line, same plate/day). Do not use a same-well VUAA1 injection as the denominator. Following [2] , treat R norm ≤ 0.05 as zero, and remove outliers by Grubbs’ test. R = ( F max − F 0 ) / F 0 Raw relative response. Not an absolute Ca 2+ concentration. Zboray et al. denote R as Δ F . R norm = R VOC / mean( R VUAA1 , line, plate/day) VOC responses are normalized to the mean 50 µM VUAA1 response of the corresponding OR cell line measured on the same plate/day. AeroSense experimental protocols Record assembled11October2026 from the website’s documented methods. This is not a claim that every specified assay was executed. Status and missing metadata remain adjacent to each protocol. Shared microscopy record: WL-MIC-01. The acquisition date/operator and delivery method have not been recovered. The 11 October methods record is otherwise retained; the live methods page carries later execution-status updates. Live methods page · Measurement and calibration audit · Results and source data A01 Molecular cloning Maintain sample identity from a bacterial colony to the plasmid preparation used downstream. Three colony-plate photographs and four DNA gels document the bacterial preparation track. 01 Transform Introduce the plasmid and retain plate identity 02 Miniprep Recover plasmid DNA from a selected colony 03 DNA gel Inspect preparation quality with a documented lane map Transformation and colony selection The existing specification uses E. coli DH5α, LB and ampicillin selection (100 µg/mL), with overnight propagation at 37 °C and 180 rpm. The supplied plate photographs retain the original labels and marked colonies. Competent-cell preparation, DNA input, transformation and recovery settings, and the corresponding negative-control record are not yet documented. View the three original plate photographs . Plasmid miniprep Link each picked colony to its construct and preparation identifier. Record the purification method, culture input, elution volume, concentration and purity. The current source does not identify the miniprep kit or provide a measured yield. The earlier endotoxin-free maxiprep specification remains a separate requirement for mammalian transfection-quality DNA. DNA gel electrophoresis Undigested plasmids were loaded as paired sample lanes for ORCO, GCaMP6f and ten OR labels. All four gels used the same 1 kb ladder. Adjacent lanes sharing a construct name are grouped in the figure, retaining their original left-to-right order. The original TIFFs are retained. Each panel uses a contiguous crop and a small rigid rotation to align the wells. The original 0–255 intensity range is unchanged; no lanes are spliced and no bands are retouched. Crop coordinates and rotation angles accompany the figure downloads. These are undigested plasmids: their migration depends on conformation as well as length. The ladder product is unknown, so individual bands are not assigned kb values. Gel concentration, running buffer, voltage and loading amount are not recorded. Dates and lane maps are retained in the Notebook. [1] Construct provenance and sequence checks The earlier preparation specification names chemically synthesised, pre-cloned pcDNA3.1(+) constructs from GenScript. Its construct count must be reconciled with the Parts — wiki page publication pending record and the labels in the image dataset. Compare returned sequences with the designs, retain both insertion junctions and internal Sanger coverage, and include a read across the (GGGGS) 3 linker. The specification advises against PstI diagnostic digests because of internal coding-sequence sites. These are verification requirements, not a declaration that every supplied colony passed. The earlier electroporation specification and Lipofectamine/P3000 workbook are not enough to identify the delivery method used for WL-MIC-01. OR plasmid : Orco plasmid DNA mass ratio 2:1 (not protein stoichiometry) Buffer Low-conductivity electroporation/nucleofection buffer, 100 µL Recovery Pre-warmed DMEM + 10 % FBS, no antibiotics Method The earlier specification calls for suspension electroporation using the DNA mass, plasmid DNA mass ratio, buffer volume, and recovery medium in the table.
              Pulse voltage, pulse number, instrument programme, cuvette, and named buffer are not specified in this source. Zboray et al. used FuGene HD into HEK293 stable lines [2] . That is not substituted for the AeroSense transfection specification above. Controls & critical notes Buffer-only pulse — electroporation toxicity. GFP-only plasmid — transfection efficiency. Genetic control Orco–GCaMP6f alone, without a tuning OR — should respond to VUAA1 but not to VOCs. Use endotoxin-free, low-salt, concentrated DNA. Use healthy log-phase cells and minimise time in electroporation buffer. Recover immediately in warm antibiotic-free medium. See Design — wiki page publication pending · See Notebook Read the corresponding evidence → B03 Stable-line selection Select G418-resistant mammalian lines after transfection. Partially executed. A separate G418 batch was reported in progress; no selection trajectory or endpoint dataset is archived. Current experimental status. The supplied fluorescence images were acquired approximately 44–48 h after transfection, before G418 selection. A separate batch is undergoing G418 selection. Consequently, these images cannot establish enrichment or survival after selection, and the schedule below remains a protocol target rather than a confirmed result for the imaged batch. Current protocol target — not a validated kill curve Protocol target timeline. Day 0 transfection with antibiotic-free recovery. G418 at 100 micrograms per millilitre starts 24 to 48 hours later and runs for 2 weeks. Concentration is then raised to 150 for 1 week, then maintenance at about 75 ongoing. These doses are a literature-informed starting condition, not an AeroSense-confirmed kill-curve result. Day 0 Transfection Suspension transfection. Recovery in DMEM + 10 % FBS, no antibiotics for 24 h. 24–48 h G418 100 µg/mL Selection start, 2 weeks. Not added at seeding. Days 1–2: little visible effect; 3–5: bulk death; 10–14: resistant colonies. After 2 weeks G418 150 µg/mL Selection raised, 1 week. Thereafter G418 ~75 µg/mL Maintenance, ongoing. Figure 2. G418 selection timeline (protocol target). Current protocol target / literature-informed starting condition: G418 started 24–48 h after transfection at 100 µg/mL for 2 weeks, then 150 µg/mL for 1 week, then maintenance at ~75 µg/mL.
                  This is not an AeroSense-validated kill-curve result. Key parameters Stage G418 concentration Duration Selection start (24–48 h post-transfection) 100 µg/mL 2 weeks Selection raised 150 µg/mL 1 week Maintenance ~75 µg/mL ongoing Method Before transfection, run a G418 kill curve on untransfected host cells (draft range 0–800 µg/mL) for that cell lot, confluence, and G418 batch. Do not treat the table below as a confirmed effective dose. After transfection, allow 24–48 h recovery. Do not add G418 at seeding. Start selection at 100 µg/mL G418 for 2 weeks. Refresh selection medium every 2–3 days. Raise G418 to 150 µg/mL for 1 week. Maintain lines at ~75 µg/mL G418 thereafter. During the first selection window, little visible effect is expected for 1–2 days, bulk cell death at days 3–5, and discrete resistant colonies against a cleared background by days 10–14. Those timings are operational expectations, not recorded AeroSense outcomes. Controls & critical notes Negative control Untransfected well at the same G418 dose throughout selection — every cell in it should die. Add G418 24–48 h after transfection, not at seeding, so cells can recover and express NeoR. The 100 → 150 → ~75 µg/mL schedule is a current protocol target / literature-informed starting condition, not an experimentally confirmed AeroSense kill curve. Partially executed. Fixed-cell endpoint imaging was acquired; the localization and time-resolved functional tests below remain assay specifications. Current microscopy record The team confirms that the supplied HEK293 images were acquired approximately 44–48 h after transfection and before G418 selection. Cells were fixed with 2% paraformaldehyde before DAPI staining, without a permeabilization step. Blue images show DAPI. Files sharing the same field number refer to the same field of view across channels; exposure was held constant within each channel across groups, and blank calibration was performed. Fixation duration, numerical exposure settings and the complete acquisition log have not been supplied. The available fields are technical observations from one experimental batch, with no independent biological repeats and no live/dead assay. DAPI provides a nuclear denominator for an image-based estimate after segmentation quality control; it does not establish viability. Dense or overlapping nuclei require explicit uncertainty handling. Report the number of analyzable fields per sample and distinguish a nuclear-normalized reporter-positive fraction from confirmed live-cell transfection efficiency. GCaMP6f resting fluorescence and mCherry expression are interpreted separately from stimulus-dependent response and cell viability. Controls & critical notes Expression control Mock / untransfected cells for mCherry autofluorescence. Functional positive control VUAA1 versus vehicle. VUAA1 is a synthetic Orco agonist used as a functional positive-control stimulus, not a proof of membrane trafficking. Concentration, solvent, incubation, antibody, and whether either assay is in the AeroSense SOP are not specified. GCaMP6f is dim at rest. Absence of bright green is expected, not a failure. See Design — wiki page publication pending · See Results · See Notebook Read the corresponding evidence → B05 Endpoint microscopy and image analysis Reproduce the DAPI-object fluorescence screen reported in Results. Executed analysis. All 25 fields and all 2,624 eligible objects are retained in the published data tables and reproducibility package. Source data and experimental context The host was HEK293, as confirmed by the team. Imaging occurred approximately 44–48 h after transfection and before G418. The team fixed cells with 2% paraformaldehyde (PFA), performed no permeabilization step, and then stained with DAPI. The source workbook contains plate-layout and reagent-calculation records, including DAPI/G418 layouts and lipid-reagent mixtures. These records do not independently establish experimental execution or an assay outcome; the VUAA1/odor grids contain labels without response measurements. The workbook does not supply objective, numerical aperture, camera model, gain, acquisition software, DAPI concentration, fixation duration, or field coordinates. Neither the source TIFF tags nor the workbook establishes these missing acquisition details. The biological preparation and transfection record is linked from Experiments ; undocumented settings are not reconstructed from a literature protocol. Conservative DAPI segmentation The BLUE plane was extracted from each exported TIFF. A 3 × 3 median filter was used for segmentation only, followed by a common threshold of >128 on the 0–255 export scale and 8-connected labeling. The bottom-right annotation rectangle (x ≥85% of image width and y ≥90% of image height) was excluded equally in every field. Eligible objects had area 200–2200 pixels, bounding-box aspect ratio ≤2.5, and object area/bounding-box area ≥0.4. Objects within 49 pixels of a frame edge or whose measurement neighborhood intersected the annotation exclusion were rejected. No watershed split was imposed on merged objects. These rules define a conservative image-analysis subset, not a validated nuclear census. Segmentation has been visually inspected, but not benchmarked against independently annotated cell boundaries. Small touching nuclei or nuclear fragments can still pass these geometric filters, so an accepted object is not guaranteed to equal one cell. DAPI is a nuclear counterstain commonly used with fixed preparations. Here, fixation is confirmed and no permeabilization was performed; completeness and uniformity of nuclear labeling were not independently assessed. Fixed DAPI images do not recover the cells’ viability before fixation. [4] Reporter measurement and positivity threshold The full Measurement record adds an explicit statistical specification, all three same-batch blank-field holdouts and the area-versus-object audit. These additions leave the original segmentation and primary thresholds unchanged. For each eligible object, the signal region contains its nuclear mask plus pixels within 12 pixels, assigned to the nearest blue connected component to limit sharing between adjacent objects. The local background is sampled 24–48 pixels from that object, excluding blue foreground; at least 100 background pixels are required. For RED and GREEN separately, the score is the signal region’s 90th percentile intensity minus the background median. Measurements use the original exported channel values, before the display adjustments. This nearest-DAPI expansion does not segment cell boundaries. Excluding blue foreground from the background ring also does not exclude every neighboring cell’s cytoplasm. Fluorescent cytoplasm within that ring can raise the estimated background and reduce an object's score, particularly in dense fields. The primary positivity threshold is the maximum of the three blank-field 99th percentiles of these object scores: RED >16.60 DN and GREEN >11.95 DN . DN denotes the 8-bit exported digital value. Alternative P95 and P99.5 blank thresholds are reported for sensitivity analysis. Thresholds are calibrated and evaluated using the same blank set, so the blank fraction is a calibration diagnostic, not an independent false-positive validation. The reported fraction is 100 × positive eligible objects / all eligible objects. Condition summaries pool these counts across fields; they do not average percentages with different denominators. “Both” indicates both channel criteria within one object's measurement region. It does not prove two-plasmid delivery, protein localization, or co-expression in a viable cell. Image processing and presentation Original TIFF and workbook files were opened read-only and verified by SHA-256 checksums. New figures use fixed linear display windows across all conditions: DAPI 0–255, GREEN 0–120 and RED 0–180; brightfield remains 0–255. The enhanced display can clip bright exported values and is used only for viewing. Original-level views remain available. No sharpening, deconvolution, content removal, generative enhancement or reconstruction of missing detail was applied. The same-field RGB merges combine the original channel positions; no registration correction was imposed. [5] [6] Web previews are resized with Lanczos resampling and saved as lossless WebP. The original scale bars remain within the full field; they were not used to infer pixel size. Object overlays mark classifications on a dimmed merge for legibility and have full-resolution PNG versions for audit.               Plate geometry, buffer volumes, and the two-round injection sequence below follow that published assay design. Key parameters Parameter Value Plate format Black-wall, clear-bottom 384-well Seeding 12,000–18,000 cells per well, 48–72 h before measurement Assay volume 20 µL assay buffer per well Vehicle injection 7 µL plain VOC buffer Odorant injection 9 µL of VOC at 4× final concentration Final well volume 36 µL (20 + 7 + 9) VOC concentrations 1, 10 and 100 µM final VUAA1 reference 50 µM on every plate for every cell line Instrument Multimode plate reader with a two-channel injector (model not specified) Readout ex 485 nm / em 535 nm Sampling F 0 for 5 s; then 30 s at 1 read/s after each injection Buffers Component Assay buffer VOC buffer NaCl 140 mM 140 mM KCl 5 mM 5 mM CaCl 2 2 mM 2 mM MgCl 2 1 mM 1 mM HEPES-Na 5 mM 5 mM Glucose 20 mM 31 mM DMSO — 0.1 % pH / osmolarity 7.3 / 340 mOsm 7.3 / 340 mOsm Method Read on a multimode plate reader with a two-channel injector, ex 485 nm / em 535 nm. Seed cells at 12,000–18,000 per well in black-wall, clear-bottom 384-well plates, 48–72 h before measurement. On the day of measurement, replace growth medium with 20 µL assay buffer per well. Round 1 — vehicle: record baseline F 0 for 5 s, inject 7 µL plain VOC buffer, record 30 s at 1 read/s. Round 2 — odorant: into the same wells, inject 9 µL of VOC at 4× final concentration, same recording protocol. Layout: one compound per row; up to eight cell lines per 24-column plate. Use three wells per cell line and measure each VOC–OR pair on at least three separate days. The volumes are self-consistent: 20 + 7 = 27 µL, then + 9 = 36 µL; 9/36 = 1/4, so a 4× stock dilutes exactly to 1× final. The vehicle injection simultaneously establishes the volume for the second round and measures the solvent and injection artefact alone. Well volume and two-round sequence Three well volumes. First: 20 microlitres assay buffer. Second: 20 plus 7 microlitres vehicle equals 27. Third: 27 plus 9 microlitres of 4 times VOC equals 36. Nine divided by 36 equals one quarter, so a 4 times stock becomes 1 times final. 20 µL assay buffer 20 µL + 7 µL vehicle 20 µL assay buffer = 27 µL + 9 µL 4× VOC 7 µL vehicle 20 µL assay buffer = 36 µL 9 / 36 = 1/4  →  4× stock dilutes to 1× final Round 1 F 0 5 s Inject 7 µL vehicle Record 30 s at 1 read/s Round 2 Same wells Inject 9 µL 4× VOC Record 30 s at 1 read/s Figure 3. Normalise to the mean VUAA1 response of that line, not a same-well VUAA1 injection. Specificity control Ca 2+ -free condition. Zboray et al. showed that Ca 2+ -free and Ca 2+ -free + EGTA buffers abolish the VUAA1 response [2] . Keep DMSO identical in VOC, vehicle, and VUAA1 wells. CaCl 2 in the assay buffer is required. Take F 0 as the 5 s baseline before the relevant injection. Take F max as the peak in the post-injection window. Compute R = (F max − F 0 ) / F 0 .
